articles.title: Feds announce $4.7B for new VIA Rail cars to be built in Ontario, Québec
articles.summary: In the latest push of its Buy Canadian Policy, the federal government is spending more than $4.7 billion for Via Rail to acquire and maintain 313 new passenger rail cars from Alstom Canada. This will…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks at the Alstom Plant in Thunder Bay, Ont. on Sept. 3 after announcing a $4.7 billion contract to build 313 new passenger cars for Via Rail. (David Jackson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Thunder Bay·New

In the latest push of its Buy Canadian Policy, the federal government is spending more than $4.7 billion for Via Rail to acquire and maintain 313 new passenger rail cars from Alstom Canada. This will be the first time in four decades that Via Rail passenger cars will be built entirely in Canada.
Contract marks first time in 4 decades that VIA Rail cars will be built entirely in Canada
Carney announces $4.7B to build rail cars in Canada instead of U.S.
In the latest push of its Buy Canadian Policy, the federal government is spending more than $4.7 billion for Via Rail to acquire and maintain 313 new passenger rail cars from Alstom Canada.
This will be the first time in four decades that Via Rail passenger cars will be built entirely in Canada. Much of its existing fleet was built in the United States.

“They'll be Canadian electricians that install the wiring, Canadian machinists that will make the precision parts, Canadian welders will build the steel frames from Canadian carbon steel," Carney said at the Alstom Plant in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Thursday morning.
“That work reaches well beyond the factory floor into communities across our country.”
These cars will be manufactured and assembled in Thunder Bay and La Pocatière, Que., with design and engineering work taking place in Saint-Bruno-de-Montarville, Que.
The government projects the project could generate more than $1.6 billion for the economy and support nearly 700 jobs across Ontario and Quebec.
“We've announced the contract of the decade,” said Michael Keroullé, president and CEO of Alstom Americas.

“This is actually kind of the first time we get the opportunity to work with the national railroad, with Via Rail. But more importantly, we are replacing cars that are now 70 years of age, very old, long overdue in terms of replacement.”

items: Carney dismisses 'unelected' Trump officials' explanation for why trade talks fell apart

blocks.text: The announcement comes on the heels of another big project underway at the plant, which will handle the final assembly of new subway cars for the Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) — each of which will include 55 per cent Canadian content.
More to come.

Sarah Law is a CBC News reporter based in Thunder Bay, Ont., and has also worked for newspapers and online publications elsewhere in the province. Have a story tip? You can reach her at sarah.law@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Far-right Israeli minister outlines plan for removal of all Palestinians from Gaza
articles.summary:
Itamar Ben-Gvir claims proposal for illegal forced displacement of 2 million people is ‘realistic’ and ‘concrete’

Israel’s far-right national security minister has set out a plan for the…

blocks.text: Israel’s far-right national security minister has set out a plan for the illegal forced expulsion of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, with the intention of sending them abroad.

Speaking in the run-up to close-fought Israeli elections, Itamar Ben-Gvir said the plan aimed to remove 250,000 Palestinians from Gaza in the first year, followed by the rest of its population of roughly 2 million over the next six years.
“It’s realistic,” Ben-Gvir said, claiming there were countries that were “ready” to take in Palestinians from Gaza, without naming which ones.

While the forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva conventions, Israeli political figures have competed over the harshness of their visions for Gaza, rebuffing efforts by the US president, Donald Trump, to advance a half-baked and largely moribund ceasefire deal that has been marked by continuing Israeli attacks.

Ben-Gvir said the far-right Jewish Power party would demand “a ministry in charge of emigration” during the formation of the next government, adding that his plan was “the result of a year and a half of work and … is concrete”.

blocks.caption: Ben-Gvir speaks at a rally in the Israeli city of Netanya this week. Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty Images

blocks.text: The proposal is contained in a euphemistically titled 20-page document titled National Work Plan for Voluntary Emigration from the Gaza Strip.

Despite the use of the word “voluntary”, the plan will be seen as coercive by the international community because of the dire conditions imposed on Gaza’s population by Israel and because of Ben-Gvir’s explicit intention: to remove Gaza’s Palestinian population.
Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

Ben-Gvir’s comments follow hard on the heels of comments by Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, who said Israel was seeking the approval of the Trump administration to displace Palestinians from Gaza, which he claimed was still under discussion after being “frozen” by Trump.
Katz, at a conference hosted by the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, said Israel would facilitate the emigration “by any means”, implying a policy of coercion.

Trump himself provoked international outrage at the beginning of his second term with a suggestion that all 2 million Palestinians leave Gaza and that the US redevelop the territory, a proposal he later walked back.

With elections in Israel in October, Ben-Gvir has made a series of inflammatory interventions aimed at his far-right base, including sharing footage from a site where Palestinians convicted of deadly attacks by Israeli military courts – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – are to be executed. In another video, he revelled in the mistreatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli custody.

Polling suggests that Jewish Power, the party led by Ben-Gvir – who has convictions for incitement to racism and support for a terrorist organisation, and who has been put under sanctions by various countries – would gain about seven seats.

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for his part staged a visit to a military outpost in Gaza on Wednesday to insist that Israel would not withdraw from the areas of Gaza that it occupies.

“We are not withdrawing. We are staying on this line. We control 60% of the strip. And there is still more to come, because we are eliminating the terrorists who threaten us – we do this day in and day out,” he said.
According to Israel’s deputy chief of general staff, Maj Gen Tamir Yadai, the country now controls 65% of Gaza. This is far beyond the 53% agreed under the ceasefire brokered last year by Trump.

As well as pushing for the expulsion of Gaza’s population, Ben-Gvir has called for the deportation of two MPs and others “who are disloyal to the state of Israel” – including Jews – saying he would promote such a policy if he is included in the next government.

articles.title: BFP urges proactive evacuations amid inclement weather
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) has urged residents in flood-prone areas to prioritize early evacuation as the country continues to experience the rainy season. During the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) has urged residents in flood-prone areas to prioritize early evacuation as the country continues to experience the rainy season.

During the Department of the Interior and Local Government’s (DILG) Kapihan forum Thursday, Fire Supt. Anthony Arroyo, chief of the BFP Public Information Service, said proactive measures remain crucial to preventing loss of life, particularly in low-lying areas prone to flooding.
“The most important thing there is really taking proactive measures,” Arroyo said.
He said authorities are anticipating the need for residents in flood-prone communities to evacuate before conditions worsen.
However, the BFP official acknowledged that authorities continue to encounter resistance from some residents who are being urged to leave their homes.
He said the BFP is working with other law enforcement agencies, local government units and the DILG to ensure vulnerable communities are properly evacuated.
For residents who cannot evacuate on their own, Arroyo said the BFP will conduct rescue operations and transport them to safer areas.
“If they are unable to evacuate, that is when rescue operations will be conducted to transport them to safe areas using our water assets,” he said. — Rendell Ivan Manuel, INQUIRER.net trainee /das

articles.title: Tinio to Marcos: Release OP’s confidential, intel funds report
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers party-list Rep. Antonio Tinio on Thursday challenged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to disclose the Office of the President’s (OP) use of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers party-list Rep. Antonio Tinio on Thursday challenged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to disclose the Office of the President’s (OP) use of confidential and intelligence funds (CIF) starting in 2023.
His statement followed Palace press officer Claire Castro’s earlier remarks that the president is transparent about the OP’s CIF allocation of P4.56 billion under the proposed 2027 national budget.

“In what way is it transparent when the public has absolutely no idea what the Office of the President’s annual P4.55 billion in confidential and intelligence funds is being spent on, let alone the CIFs of other agencies?” he stressed.
Tinio then dared the president to release the OP’s accomplishment reports, detailing where and how the more than P18.2 billion in CIF from 2023 to 2026 was used.

“If there is indeed transparency, the President should make public the detailed quarterly accomplishment reports on the more than P18.2 billion in confidential and intelligence funds of the Office of the President from 2023 to 2026,” he added.

The solon emphasized that the same scrutiny being applied to the Office of the Vice President’s (OVP) confidential funds, which is being deliberated during the Senate impeachment trial against Vice President Sara Duterte, must also be applied to the president.

“This amount is staggering, so the public deserves an explanation. The same level of scrutiny applied to the vice president’s confidential funds should also be applied to the president’s. Otherwise, their so-called transparency is just fake news,” he said.
Tinio said that under the Constitution, government agencies with CIF are required to submit quarterly accomplishment reports detailing how the funds were used.
He further slammed Executive Secretary Ralph Recto’s claim that the Commission on Audit has issued an unmodified opinion on the OP’s financial statements.

“That is exactly what the Office of the Vice President told those questioning its confidential funds. Now, the OVP’s brazen abuse has been exposed, despite the so-called unmodified opinion,” the solon said.
The OP’s proposed 2027 budget amounted to P10.156 billion, which Recto said was 64% lower than in 2026.

The House of Representatives appropriations committee last Tuesday terminated the OP’s budget briefing in less than an hour as part of parliamentary courtesy, a move that Tinio and other minority lawmakers strongly opposed.

According to him, Congress must abolish the parliamentary courtesy tradition, stressing the importance of interpellations amid investigations into alleged anomalies in government projects involving some government officials, including Marcos. /das

articles.title: Indonesia: Thousands fall sick from free school meals
articles.summary: Hundreds of new food poisoning cases have been reported this week linked to President Prabowo Subianto's free school lunch program. The costly scheme has been dogged by health concerns and…

image.caption: Indonesia's school meal program was launched in 2025 as a signature policy of President Prabowo SubiantoImage: Muhammad Iqbal/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: More 1,700 people have contracted food poisoning in Indonesia over the past week after eating free school meals provided by the government as part of a new scheme.
At least 725 pupils and 25 teachers at a school in Lasem on the island of Java complained that they felt unwell on Thursday morning after consuming the free lunch on Wednesday.
"They had diarrhea, they were vomiting, and felt nauseous," said the school's principal. "There was a queue at the bathrooms because two of our toilets are under renovation."
Earlier this week, more than 600 students in Sidoarjo, East Java, were also taken to hospital after eating free lunch meals on Tuesday.
In two other cases on Wednesday, 49 people in the East Java city of Nganjuk and 237 in the West Sumatra region of Agam also fell ill.

blocks.caption: Children in Sidoarjo, East Java, were taken to the regional general hospitalImage: Suryanto/REUTERS

blocks.text: One lawmaker, Charles Honoris, put the total number of food poisoning cases linked to the free school meals scheme as high as 50,000 since, citing health department data.
"This is a failure of the ⁠system," he said.
What has caused the food poisoning?
The mass outbreaks of food poisoning have been blamed on improper food storage and late delivery of pre-cooked meals.
According to the school principal in Lasem, a food taster found that some of the grilled chicken to be distributed was "slimy" and therefore put aside.
"The kitchen operator said the food was cooked at 3 a.m. and it ​was eaten at noon," she reported.
President Prabowo's free school meals scheme

The $12.94 -billion (€11.13-billion) program, launched in January 2025, is one of President Prabowo Subianto's signature policies, intended to improve nutrition for up to 80 million children as well as pregnant and breastfeeding women.
But the costly scheme has been dogged by allegations of corruption, ​leadership changes and spate of mass food poisoning outbreaks.

It was among the first budget items to be cut back as the Indonesian government moved to counter the economic impact of the war in the Middle East and hundreds of people took to the streets of the capital, Jakarta, last week to call for it to be scrapped entirely.
How Indonesia aims to combat childhood malnutrition
"This has become a national alarm," said Ubaid Matraji, a researcher at the Indonesian Education Monitoring Network.
"The government cannot continue to treat them as mere statistical figures. Behind every number there is a sick child, a panicked family, and the state's failure to guarantee safe food."
The head of Indonesia's National Nutrition Agency, ⁠which oversees the scheme, told a parliamentary hearing that the food poisoning cases would be ​handled "seriously."

articles.title: At least 14 Serbians targeted with advanced spyware
articles.summary:
Student protesters among those hacked, Share Foundation says, but government denies spying

At least 14 people from across Serbian civil society were targeted with advanced spyware earlier…

blocks.text: At least 14 people from across Serbian civil society were targeted with advanced spyware earlier this year, the digital rights group Share Foundation has said.

The wave of spyware infections was discovered in August after Apple notified people in 110 ⁠countries that they had probably been victims ⁠of mercenary spyware. Share said on Wednesday it marked the largest documented ​wave of such infection in Serbia to date.

The Citizen Lab, which carries out forensic analyses of spyware attacks, released an analysis on Wednesday showing that at least one of the Serbians had been targeted with the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware, which would have given the attacker “total access to the device”.

Share said those targeted included members of a Serbian student movement that has been a thorn in the side of the government of Aleksandar Vučić since 2024. Coalescing out of countrywide protests that followed the collapse of a train station that winter, it is one of the largest student movements in Europe.
Vučić has been in power for more than a decade, during which time critics have said he has overseen a hollowing-out of institutions while steering the country closer to Moscow.

There is no evidence that Vučić’s government was the entity that targeted the students with spyware. In an interview with Euronews Serbia TV on Wednesday, Ana Brnabić, the parliamentary speaker and a ranking member of the ruling Serbian Progressive party, denied that students had been spied on. “Absolutely not,” she said. “I do not believe a single word they’ve [students, Share] said.”
Share said the timing – during March’s local elections – may have been a practice run before snap elections set for this October.

“This is the largest documented wave of surveillance in Serbia so far,” said Andrijana Ristic, a policy adviser at Share. “We imagine … that the local elections were basically used as a test for the ruling party to see [the spyware’s] strengths, but also to see the amount of pressure they are able to exert over the students and the opposition.”

John Scott-Railton, a senior researcher at The Citizen Lab, said: “Our forensic findings, and this fresh wave of Apple threat notifications reveal that Serbia’s peaceful pro-democracy movement is being aggressively targeted with mercenary spyware ahead of key 2026 election cycles.”

Milica Popović, one of the students who was targeted, called the attacks “cruel”. She said: “Thinking that someone may have entered my private space without my knowledge made me feel so exposed.” But, she said, the attack, as uncomfortable as it was, would not deter her or the student movement. “If their intention was to frighten us, or make us stop, it will not work.”

NSO Group, which makes Pegasus, a spyware that has been leveraged by authoritarian states to target journalists, human rights campaigners and dissidents, began as an Israeli company with close ties to the military.
after newsletter promotion

It is now under US ownership, and appears to be searching for a way into the US market, including through efforts to get off the US Commerce Department’s blacklist. However, this and other incidents will raise questions about what has been described as their attempt to rebrand as an “ethical spyware company”.
NSO Group has been permanently barred by a US court from targeting WhatsApp users and Meta products. It is unclear if this most recent Pegasus attack happened via WhatsApp.
“Today, Pegasus is still being used to hack people campaigning for democracy. NSO spent a decade promising reform, yet their spyware is still an instrument of political repression,” said Railton.
NSO Group was approached for comment.

articles.title: Trump's Iran strategy: Could this become a forever war?
articles.summary: The US has launched fresh attacks on military targets in Iran. It wants to prevent Tehran rebuilding its destroyed capabilities, but risks triggering a sustained downward spiral of reconstruction…

image.caption: A US fighter aircraft launches from an aircraft carrier in the Arabian Sea, August 2026Image: U.S. Navy/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: US president Donald Trump has given a fairly clear description of what the next phase of the Iran war could look like. The Iranians had tried to rebuild their radar equipment, Trump stated after the most recent wave of US strikes. "We waited until it was almost built, and then we hit it," he said.

On Tuesday, American forces once again attacked several targets in Iran. According to US Central Command (CENTCOM), the targets destroyed included "air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites."
"Mowing the grass"
Iran responded by firing rockets and drones at US facilities in the region. With this, the war moved on to what CENTCOM had indicated just a few days earlier could be the strategy for the next phase.

blocks.caption: What strategy will Donald Trump choose to pursue next in the war with Iran?Image: Ken Cedeno/REUTERS

blocks.text: According to the news portal Axios, it was considering limited strikes, at regular intervals if necessary, to prevent Iran from reconstituting its military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz. An American government representative used a concept from Israeli security policy to describe this idea: He called it "mowing the grass."

The metaphor refers to a strategy that doesn't even attempt to promise that an opponent will be defeated once and for all. It is enough to regularly reduce the enemy's military capabilities to the point where the threat remains manageable. When the grass grows back, you "mow" it again.
Applied to the situation in Iran, this would mean the US keeping an eye on which military capabilities the enemy is reconstituting, and attacking once it crosses a certain threshold.
Successes that won't last

In the past few months, the US has scored some military successes. US forces have significantly reduced Iran's military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz, and have begun clearing Iranian sea mines.

However, these successes will not last. Tehran is repairing or procuring new radar installations, anti-aircraft positions, and anti-ship missiles. US bombs could certainly destroy important Iranian positions with targeted strikes. But the knowledge and the industrial basis of Iranian military technology would remain.

blocks.caption: An image issued by US CENTCOM of a precision strike against an Iranian military target in July 2026Image: US Central Command/AFP

blocks.text: Reconstruction can therefore be delayed, but not prevented. The US will repeatedly be confronted with the same choice: whether to accept that Tehran is regaining its capabilities, or to attack again and destroy them.

Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Washington, warned as early as April that this development could lead to an "enduring low-intensity conflict punctuated by more intensive interventions."
Trump's belligerent warnings

The fact that the strategy of "mowing the grass" is reaching its limits is also because it was never designed for a war with a state. Israel developed the strategy to combat non-state actors likeHamas.

However, as Yacoubian pointed out in her article, the Israeli academics who initially coined the term warned that if the opponent had "statist characteristics and/or more powerful capabilities, 'mowing the grass' might become an outdated military strategy." This is clearly the case with the Strait of Hormuz.

The US needs to keep the strait reliably open. Iran, on the other hand, only needs to make people believe that the passage remains dangerous. In this way, even a significantly weakened opponent can impose substantial costs on Washington.

blocks.caption: Keeping the vital shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz open is a priority for the USImage: Atta Kenare/AFP

blocks.text: Another problem for the US is that, while Washington can determine the intensity of its own attacks, it has no control over Tehran's response. This week, US president Trump warned Tehran not to launch a retaliatory strike, threatening that Iran would be "totally wiped out as a country" if it did.

Nonetheless, the regime in Tehran immediately fired missiles against American facilities in the region. Jordan alone reported 13 ballistic missiles in its airspace, 10 of which it was able to intercept.
The nuclear question

But Mona Yacoubian believes that repeated American attacks carry a far greater risk. She warns that they may lead Tehran to conclude that "pursuit of a nuclear weapon" is the only way to achieve "lasting deterrence." This suggests that, by attacking Iran, the US and Israel could actually accelerate the precise development they sought to bring under control.

blocks.caption: The Natanz nuclear facility in Iran was one of the first sites targeted by the US and IsraelImage: Planet Labs

blocks.text: From Washington's perspective, the alternatives available to Trump don't look much better. If the president accepts Iran rebuilding its military strength around the Strait of Hormuz, he risks renewed attacks on shipping and disruption of one of the world's most important energy routes.

The consequences for the global economy are well known. In spite of the upheaval and repeated negotiations, a political agreement between Washington and Tehran has so far failed because of apparently insurmountable differences.
The next "forever war"?

For Donald Trump, "mowing the grass" has domestic appeal, in spite of the uncertainty it brings to foreign policy. The US president would be able to avoid occupation, nation building, and deploying large numbers of American ground troops. At the same time, it allows him to distance himself from the so-called "forever wars" he repeatedly accused his predecessors in the White House of pursuing.

Ultimately, though, this supposed way of avoiding a forever war could become one of its own. Yacoubian describes it as a "Sisyphean attrition strategy without end." As long as Washington is not prepared at some point to accept the rebuilding of Iran's capabilities, each successful attack merely creates the justification for the next one.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Watch: Gloria Steinem dedicated her life to fight for women's equality
articles.summary: The feminist icon who became leader of the women's liberation movement in the US died on Wednesday at the age of 92, according to her foundation.

blocks.text: Gloria Steinem spent more than 60 years as one of the most prominent voices in the fight for women's rights.
She launched herself into the mainstream in the 1960s with an expose of New York City's Playboy Club, documenting the harsh conditions she faced working undercover as a Playboy Bunny.
A powerful and outspoken campaigner at a time of routine discrimination, Steinem faced sexist criticism and harassment from men throughout her long career.
Her lifelong battle saw many victories, including the US Supreme Court's 1973 Roe v Wade decision that guaranteed a woman's right to an abortion.
It also saw setbacks, like that same decision being overturned in 2022.
The feminist icon died on Wednesday at the age of 92, her foundation said in a statement. She never retired.

articles.title: Bank of Canada unveils new vertical $20 bill featuring King Charles
articles.summary: This is the first Canadian paper currency to feature Charles, whose image replaces that of the late Queen Elizabeth II.

image.caption: Canada's new $20 bill was unveiled Thursday by the Bank of Canada. (The Bank of Canada)

blocks.text: Canada·New
This is the first Canadian paper currency to feature Charles, whose image replaces that of the late Queen Elizabeth II.
The bill will enter circulation in 2027
It's official — Canada has a new $20 bill.

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem unveiled the new, vertical bill featuring a portrait of King Charles on Thursday in Ottawa. It's the first Canadian paper currency to feature Charles, whose image replaces that of the late Queen Elizabeth II.
In a press conference, Macklem called the unveiling "historic," and added the new bill is both "visually stunning and more secure than ever."
The new note is polymer, predominantly green and vertical in orientation. The Canadian National Vimy Memorial remains on the back. Charles is centred on the front.
The new note will gradually enter circulation in late February 2027.
The Bank of Canada has previously noted that the $20 bill is its most-circulated currency.

This is also the second bank note in the bank's vertical series. The first, the $10 note, features civil rights pioneer and businesswoman Viola Desmond. That bill won won the coveted Bank Note of the Year Award for 2018, beating out top designs from places like Switzerland, Norway, Russia and the Solomon Islands.

items: King Charles won't be featured on $20 bills until 2027, Bank of Canada says
Donald Trump mistakes Bank of Canada for retail bank

blocks.text: The government announced that King Charles would replace his mother on Canada's currency during his coronation celebration in 2023. The first Canadian coins bearing the image of the King began circulating that December.
The reigning monarch has been featured on Canadian bills since 1935.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: PNP backs strict enforcement of no-build zones amid flood risks
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Thursday said it would assist local government units (LGUs) and concerned government agencies in enforcing no-build zones and other…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Thursday said it would assist local government units (LGUs) and concerned government agencies in enforcing no-build zones and other safety measures in flood-prone and hazardous areas.

This followed President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s call for stricter enforcement of “no-build zone” policies and other measures to reduce flooding and protect communities from the effects of climate change.

According to PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr., police units would provide assistance when needed to maintain peace and order and ensure public safety during enforcement operations in the “no-build zones.”

“The PNP will support local government units and concerned agencies in the lawful enforcement of no-build zones, particularly when police assistance is needed to maintain peace and order and ensure public safety,” Nartatez said in a statement.
He also said police assistance in these operations would remain focused on enforcing the law and protecting the public.
“Our police units will remain professional and impartial. We will perform our duties based on the law and will not allow political considerations to compromise public safety,” he said.
Nartatez also said police commanders had been directed to coordinate with local authorities, monitor areas identified as danger zones, and provide immediate assistance when necessary.

He urged residents and local officials to comply with existing laws and safety regulations, particularly in communities vulnerable to flooding and other hazards. — Rendell Ivan Manuel, INQUIRER.net trainee /das

articles.title: Israel prepared to remove Palestinians from Gaza if U.S. approves, defence minister says
articles.summary: Israel is waiting for U.S. approval to remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, Defence Minister Israel Katz said, renewing a plan that has been widely condemned as forced displacement and described…

image.caption: Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said at a Wednesday news conference that the Israeli government is 'organized and prepared' to remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip 'by sea, by air, by every way possible.' (Aggelos Nakkas/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

Israel is waiting for U.S. approval to remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, Defence Minister Israel Katz said, renewing a plan that has been widely condemned as forced displacement and described as ethnic cleansing.
Officials describe move as 'voluntary' but Palestinians fear forced expulsion, which would be war crime

Israel is waiting for U.S. approval to remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Wednesday, resurfacing a plan that has been widely condemned as forced displacement and described as ethnic cleansing.

Katz, speaking at a news conference hosted by Israeli news site Ynet and newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, said Israel is ready to facilitate what has been described as "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians in Gaza "by any means."
Palestinians in Gaza have mostly rejected the idea, fearing it will result in their forced expulsion.

Yedioth Ahronoth reported that Israeli National Security Minister and far-right Jewish Power party leader Itamar Ben-Gvir will unveil the plan on Thursday, which will reportedly remove Palestinians over the span of seven years.

Ben-Gvir — who has been sanctioned by Ottawa over repeated incitements of violence against Palestinian communities — is expected to present the plan dubbed "Disengagement 710" as part of his campaign in October's legislative elections.
Pending U.S. backing, Katz described the move as necessary, insisting the issue at hand is finding countries to take the Palestinians in.
"There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration," Katz said.
Katz said the Israeli government "is organized and prepared to get them out — by sea, by air, by every way possible," according to the Times of Israel.

The comments come nearly three years since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel, which killed 1,200 people and led to about 250 being taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies. Israel's ensuing assault on Gaza has killed more than 73,400, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, and left much of the enclave in ruins.

In February 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump pitched the idea of taking ownership of the territory and permanently displacing its residents before turning it into the "Riviera of the Middle East," which at the time was met with unified anger and concern.

Trump later appeared to abandon the idea, and in January 2026 established the "Board of Peace" to ostensibly handle the resolution of violence and reconstruction in Gaza, although the board has made little progress.
Katz claims Trump has not abandoned the plan, but has merely "frozen it" due to pressure from Arab states, the Times of Israel reported.
Forcible deportation 'manifestly illegal': UN
In response to Trump's remarks in February 2025, United Nations experts warned that moving or forcibly relocating Palestinians would violate international law.

"It is manifestly illegal to invade and annex foreign territory by force, to forcibly deport its population, and to deprive the Palestinian people of their inalienable right to self-determination," they said in 2025.

The UN Office of the High Commissioner raised concern over ethnic cleansing by Israeli authorities in both Gaza and the West Bank this past February. It said the increase of reported attacks and forcible transfers "appear aimed at a permanent displacement of Palestinians throughout the occupied territories."

Many Palestinians in Gaza refuse to leave their homes despite dire living conditions after Israel's two-year offensive in the enclave left roughly two million people displaced and living in crowded makeshift tent camps. Families have been left to deal with widespread destruction, severe water shortages and acute food insecurity.

"We were born and raised in Gaza, we will die and be buried in Gaza," Umm Yusuf Shabat, a 55-year-old mother and grandmother, told a freelance videographer with CBC News in the legislative district west of Gaza City.
"There is no immigration by any means. It is enough, the displacement we went through. No matter what happens, we will not [be displaced] again."
Muhammad Abu Jibbeh, 39, echoed Shabat's remarks, saying he refuses to leave.
"Ultimately, this is our homeland … we are going to remain steadfast and we will not leave our land and we utterly reject the idea of leaving the country or migrating," Abu Jibbeh said.
Gaza stuck in ‘humanitarian purgatory’ 9 months into ceasefire

Others say the living conditions have made it impossible to bear or envision a future in the war-torn territory. The Israel Defence Forces currently control up to 70 per cent of Gaza, according to Israeli sources cited in a July report.
Abdul Rahman Al-Turk, 28, says he has been displaced seven times within Gaza since the war began in October 2023. He says water and bread shortages persist, making it difficult to get by.
"We are tired. When we have the first chance to leave the country, we will take it," Al-Turk told CBC News.
"There is no future here. There is no work, no construction, nothing. What do we want to do in this country? If the solution is migration, then get us out."
Latest Trump plan notes no displacement

Despite a U.S.-backed ceasefire that took effect in October 2025, which halted the large-scale fighting that had devastated the enclave, Israeli strikes and raids continue in Gaza. The Gaza Health Ministry said more than 1,300 civilians have died since then.
The 20-point peace plan, agreed upon by Israel and Hamas in October 2025, did not call for Palestinians’ displacement.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected Trump's new 15-point peace plan last month, saying Israel will not withdraw forces until Hamas ⁠⁠fully disarms. Trump's plan states that nobody will be forced to leave the Gaza Strip under Clause 13, which calls for a phased Israeli withdrawal.
Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point Gaza peace plan
Hamas formally dissolved its primary civilian governing body in July but maintains it will only disarm after a complete Israeli withdrawal from the territory.
Katz's remarks this week drew a sharp rebuke from Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who condemned the plan.

"After our trip to the Gaza-Egypt border last year, [Sen. Jeff Merkley] and I released a report entitled, 'The Netanyahu Government is Implementing a Plan to Ethnically Cleanse Gaza of Palestinians,'" Van Hollen said in a post on X.
"Now the Israeli [Ministry] of Defence confirmed that's the goal. We must end our complicity."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sara Jabakhanji is a Toronto-based senior writer assigned to cover news developments in the Middle East. She has worked in CBC bureaus in Ottawa, London and Toronto. You can reach her at sara.jabakhanji@cbc.ca.
With files from Mohamed El Saife

articles.title: Hiker missing from B.C. gondola made call to 911 saying he's 'stuck on the mountain'
articles.summary: Search and rescue crews say a hiker who's been missing from the Squamish area since Sunday managed to briefly get through to 911 on Tuesday, but that searchers still haven't been able to find him.

image.caption: Stanislav Volo was last seen getting off the Sea-to-Sky Gondola on Sunday, Aug. 30. (Yana Geng, Squamish RCMP)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Search and rescue crews say a hiker who's been missing from the Squamish area since Sunday managed to briefly get through to 911 on Tuesday, but that searchers still haven't been able to find him.
Stanislav Volo vanished on Sunday after going on a hike above the Sea-to-Sky Gondola
A new development has come to light in the search for a missing Squamish man who vanished while hiking by himself in B.C.'s Sea-to-Sky region.
Stanislav Volo got off at the top of the Sea-to-Sky Gondola, in Squamish, around 11:30 a.m. PT on Sunday, with plans to hike the Mount Habrich Loop, according to RCMP.
Dozens of volunteers from multiple search and rescue crews around the Lower Mainland have converged on the mountain above the gondola since to search for the missing 43-year-old.
Drones, helicopters, ground crews and police dogs have all been involved in the effort.

items: Crews scour mountains for missing hiker who took Sea-to-Sky gondola

blocks.text: Volo’s sister, Ola Volo, said they received a new clue on Tuesday during the search.
“We recently got informed that he did make a phone call to 911,” Ola said. “He did say on the call that he was stuck on the mountain, but the call was very short.”
Search teams looking for missing hiker in Sea-to-Sky region
The call to 911 came through at around 6:30 p.m. on Tuesday, search and rescue confirmed.
Ola said the family listened to the phone call.
“It was definitely his phone number and his voice,” she said. “It was so brief that I just hold on to those seconds as much as I can.”
Mount Habrich Loop has limited cell service, which the family believes is the reason for the short phone call.
“We know he's out there and we know he's alive and he's doing everything he can to fight this weather and to stay warm and to stay with us,” Ola said.
Volo's cousin Yana Geng said there is a huge community of people who care about him.
“He is an amazing, hands-on, dedicated father to two beautiful children. He's a loving husband. He's a wonderful son, he's an awesome brother and an awesome cousin as well,” Geng said.
'Infinite number of places he could be'
Tyler Duncan, a search manager with Squamish Search and Rescue, said they believe Volo is still in the Habrich loop area.
“Due to the technical aspect of it, due to the countless number of gullies, little canyons, big boulder fields, there's literally an infinite number of places he could be,” Duncan said.
The area, while not geographically large, is challenging to search.
“When you actually get up there, and you look at pictures of the zone, you realize just how technical the terrain is and how varied and ledgy and stepped that terrain is,” Duncan said.
Weather complicated search efforts on Wednesday, and the search is resuming on Thursday morning for the fifth day.
On the day Volo went missing, other hikers believe they saw him on the Shannon Basin Loop, which leads to the hike he was expected to be on.
A section of the Mount Habrich Loop includes a series of fairly complicated cliff bands that stack on top of each other.
“Which is a very popular climbing area,” Duncan said. “There are some hiking trails that go up there, but it is technical, exposed alpine terrain, so not [a] beginner hiking zone.”
Duncan said there was also a missed call from Volo to his wife around 4:30 p.m. on Sunday.
“Our best theory is that he's down off the ridgeline somewhere and has lost service,” Duncan said.
Surveillance footage from Sunday shows Volo getting off the Sea-to-Sky Gondola at the top wearing a black T-shirt, black shorts and a black backpack.
Squamish RCMP are asking anyone who may have spotted Volo to contact them at
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Alanna Kelly is a CBC News journalist based in Squamish, B.C., covering the Sea-to-Sky region, including Whistler, Pemberton and the Sunshine Coast. You can email story ideas to alanna.kelly@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Sabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trial
articles.summary:
A Maltese businessman has been cleared of involvement in the journalist’s death, but his trial revealed the challenges faced by those leading the search for her killers

The conclusion of the…

blocks.text: The conclusion of the longest-running murder trial in Maltese history has left a country in turmoil, and a grieving family still searching for answers.

At 7.30pm on Wednesday, gasps and cheers echoed around hall 22 of the courts of justice in Valletta, as a jury pronounced a businessman accused of ordering the murder of the investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia not guilty.

Yorgen Fenech, 44, had been facing a life sentence if convicted. Now, after nearly seven years in and out of custody, he is free to return to a gilded life as the heir to one of Malta’s biggest fortunes.

In her reporting, Caruana Galizia had taken aim at many powerful figures, including Fenech and the politicians he was close to. Her revelations, and the fallout from her violent death in a car bombing in October 2017, had ultimately led to the resignation of the prime minister, Joseph Muscat, and several members of his government.

Within weeks, three hitmen accused of planting the bomb were arrested. Two were sentenced to life in prison after pleading guilty to murder, while the third was given a reduced 15-year sentence in exchange for evidence against his accomplices.
After Wednesday’s decision, the long search for whoever was responsible for hiring them must begin again.

The opposition leader, Alex Borg, has demanded the recall of parliament from its summer recess, and called for the government to act to strengthen press protection and anti-corruption measures. “We believe journalism is the backbone of a democracy,” he told the Guardian, describing the failure to find the culprits as a black mark against the Labour government. The party has been in power since 2013.
Caruana Galizia’s family described the verdict as “justice denied”.
The attorney general is considering whether to appeal for a retrial. The chances of success may be slim: Both charges brought against Fenech were dismissed by an 8-1 majority.

It had taken nine years, a relentless family campaign and a determined judge to bring Fenech before a jury. In the end, they took him at his word. During his evidence, he was adamant: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder.”

blocks.caption: Yorgen Fenech was cleared by a jury of complicity in voluntary homicide and association with the intention of committing a crime.  Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters

blocks.text: While the identity of the mastermind remains a mystery, what the trial did reveal was the full extent of the challenges faced by those leading the search for Daphne’s killers.

Witness after witness spoke of attempts to block and sabotage the murder investigation. As detectives worked to identify all of those involved, from the bomb makers to the hitmen to their ultimate client, they heard evidence that the most sensitive details were being leaked. Most disturbingly of all, the jury was told much of the information was coming from the prime minister’s right-hand man.
“Don’t worry about me, nobody can touch me,” Fenech was heard saying in secret recordings that formed a cornerstone of the case against him, and played to the jury.

blocks.caption: A court artist’s sketch of Yorgen Fenech during the trial. Illustration: Anna Calleja Day

blocks.text: The man who had made those recordings was a taxi driver, Melvin Theuma, who testified to acting as the middleman between Fenech and the bombers. He was the key prosecution witness, having secured a pardon two years after the murder in return for giving evidence.

In July 2020, he was taken to hospital in a critical condition. Overcome with remorse, he had attempted suicide while staying at a safe house, and it took intensive support to get him back in the stand.
What follows is the story of the search for those responsible, based on pre-trial hearings, the trial itself, and related court cases.
Consumed by an investigation that would kill her
In the last summer of her life, Caruana Galizia was deeply isolated.

As a younger woman, she had not only been brilliant, but strikingly beautiful, with big statement earrings and shining black hair. She had co-founded a national newspaper, was a lifestyle magazine publisher, and had become one of Malta’s most-read columnists, all while raising three sons.

blocks.caption: Daphne Caruana Galizia in 1989 at Lisbon zoo with her sons Paul, Andrew and Matthew. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

blocks.text: In later life, it was the investigative work that consumed her.
Her blog Running Commentary was among the most-read news sites in Malta, but its popularity, and her often scathing satires of public figures, made her a target.
She had as many detractors as fans, and on social media she was vilified as a “witch”. There were arson attacks, and the family dogs were killed.
“I was worried about her,” her middle son, Andrew, told the trial. “The atmosphere around her was horrible. People would stare at her in Valletta. She wouldn’t leave the house.”
Caruana Galizia knew she was at risk and had already started varying her routine. For added security, she drove a rental car.

It was in that car that she died on 16 October 2017, aged 53, metres from her house. A bomb placed under the driver’s seat ripped through the vehicle, scattering burning remains across the road and into a field.

blocks.caption: Forensic experts examine the field where a bomb blew up Daphne Caruana Galizia’s rental car. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters

blocks.text: Barricaded inside their home, sheltering from the media storm, Daphne’s sons and her widow, Peter, wondered who they could trust. They felt sure her work would hold clues, but also that they could not hand sensitive source material to the police. Her eldest son, Matthew, a software engineer who had been part of the reporting team that won a Pulitzer prize for the Panama Papers, a giant leak of offshore company data, suggested contacting journalists outside Malta.
“I didn’t have the resources to do the investigation on my own,” he told the jury at Fenech’s trial.
He reached out to the Guardian, which joined Reuters, the non-profit Forbidden Stories and others to form the Daphne Project.

Before her death, Caruana Galizia had published a series of stories that plunged the Maltese government into scandal. She had found evidence in the Panama Papers that the energy minister, Konrad Mizzi, and the prime minister’s chief of staff, a businessman turned political fixer called Keith Schembri, had set up offshore companies held via anonymous trusts. Posts she published, read out during the trial, suggested she thought they were planning to use these to receive kickbacks.

blocks.caption: Caruana Galizia’s sons Matthew, Paul and Andrew and her husband, Peter, take part in a protest march in Valletta in 2019. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters

blocks.text: Those allegations are now the subject of a criminal case, in which Fenech, Schembri, Mizzi and others are pleading not guilty to corruption, trading in influence and criminal association.

At the time she died, Caruana Galizia was receiving a leak of information about a large government contract – a concession to build a €500m gas power plant that would supply electricity for the national grid. The leak came from the servers of the company building the plant, Electrogas. One of its shareholders was Fenech, and the email traffic suggested he was a driving force, handling communications with the government, and the refinancing of a crucial bank loan.
The jury heard how, in her blog, Caruana Galizia had described the venture as a “magic new corruption power station”.

blocks.caption: Grafitti on a wall in rural Malta highlights Caruna Galizia’s murder. Photograph: Simon Leigh/Alamy

blocks.text: The prosecution had claimed, in its closing submissions, that Fenech’s motive for ordering her murder was to prevent any further revelations.

The Electrogas data was shared with the Daphne Project. As reporters combed the files, following the money trails, Keith Arnaud, a homicide detective, searched for the killers. At first he made rapid progress, thanks to the FBI. The agency’s cellphone analysis team had been in Europe when the bomb went off, and they diverted to Malta, landing there within hours.
after newsletter promotion

The hitmen, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio, and their accomplice Vincent Muscat, had used burner phones but they had been careless, often carrying them alongside their usual mobiles. The FBI made the link, tracing a text message sent by George to detonate the bomb. In December 2017, the trio were arrested.

In April 2018, Vincent Muscat told police he was ready to turn on his accomplices, in exchange for a shorter sentence. While the hitmen had never known the identity of their ultimate client, Muscat had the name of the middleman: Melvin Theuma.

blocks.caption: A makeshift memorial to Caruana Galizia in Valletta, Malta. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters

blocks.text: The mosquito and the lion

For Theuma, a fatherless teenager, the Malta Racing Club was a home from home. He started as a groom, tending to the ponies that pull small carts around the bare-earth track. Before long he was working as a scout for a bookmaker. The old betting shop still stands across the street from the Fenech family stables.

blocks.caption: Melvin Theuma, a key witness who was granted a presidential pardon, with Judge Edwina Grima visiting the site where Caruana Galizia was killed. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters

blocks.text: Theuma and Fenech became friends, but it was not a relationship of equals. As the taxi driver said in court: “I was hanging out with a lion, and I’m a mosquito.”
Police said in court they had identified Fenech as a suspect by September 2018. But it would take until February 2019 for a warrant to be authorised to intercept his calls.

The person signing the warrants was the prime minister, Joseph Muscat. From the beginning, Muscat had been receiving updates about the investigation directly from Arnaud and his colleagues. That decision was controversial because, along with his ministers, he had been one of the main subjects of Caruana Galizia’s reporting.

Muscat has indicated it was customary for the prime minister to sign warrants in cases of national importance. He has previously said he fulfilled his duties “without fear, prejudice or favour”. In a statement on Thursday, he said that from the beginning, and while he was still in office, “no one was protected from or immune to justice”.
Schembri was allowed to attend the police briefings and told the trial he was kept informed throughout.

The two men were close – Schembri had started out as Muscat’s campaign manager – but Schembri had another good friend: Fenech. They had played football together as children, and when Fenech, a few years younger, stepped up to run his family business, Schembri had mentored him. They would often holiday together and gather for family events.
Schembri is accused of repeatedly leaking sensitive details about the homicide investigation to Fenech. He denies the allegations, and is being prosecuted over the matter in a separate criminal case.

During his trial, Fenech sought to paint Schembri as the ultimate mastermind, describing himself as a go-between, passing messages to Theuma. Fenech’s lawyers depicted the taxi driver as a blackmailer and a liar, and accused the police of framing Fenech because they had failed to properly follow other leads. They said the searches at Schembri’s home and his office had been bungled. His phone, active 28 minutes before the raid, was never found.
“All roads lead to Keith and all bridges leading to Keith were burnt,” Fenech’s lawyer said. “And so a bridge had to be built to Yorgen Fenech.”
Schembri denies any involvement in the murder. In their evidence, police said he was never a murder suspect.

blocks.caption: Malta’s former chief of staff, Keith Schembri, was a close childhood friend of Yorgen Fenech. Photograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Under questioning, Fenech admitted paying €400,000, via Theuma, to the hitmen to cover their legal bills. He said this was to keep Theuma calm, and that the cab driver “drained” him of money. He also admitted giving Theuma money before the murder, but said he warned that it should not go ahead, telling the taxi driver to “stop it here”.
He admitted passing information about the police investigation from Schembri to Theuma, starting soon after the assassination.

“Keith Schembri was continuously informed and in a way you can say real time,” Fenech told a court in 2019, in a constitutional case regarding his right to a fair trial. “The information was passed to me by Keith Schembri but it came from Mr Arnaud, and he used to tell me that it came from Mr Arnaud.”

Recordings, messages and testimony from Fenech himself indicate that in the first months after the murder he had passed on to Theuma the identity of who had made the bomb and the date on which the police were planning to arrest the hitmen. When the police raided their shed by the docks, they had already thrown their mobile phones into the water, and one of them had written his wife’s number on his wrist.

In April 2018, Fenech also shared that Vincent Muscat was offering to become a witness for the prosecution. The news sent Theuma into a spin and he started to record his exchanges with Fenech, using a spare phone switched to airplane mode so it would not ring.

blocks.caption: Vincent Muscat is serving a 15-year prison sentence for his part in the murder of Caruana Galizia. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters

blocks.text: It was around this time that Arnaud’s investigation seemed to lose momentum. Eventually, details of what had been uncovered began to leak. By May 2019, reporters had Theuma’s name.

Europol, which had been supporting Arnaud and his team, threatened over the summer of 2019 to withdraw unless arrests were made. The family were also losing patience. “We had known what was being alleged about Melvin Theuma for months,” Matthew Caruana Galizia has said. “And it reached a point where I just wanted to go into the street and spraypaint his name on a wall. I wanted the world to know that he was the middleman, to just push the police into action.”
While the walls around the prime minister and his friends looked strong from the outside, when the police finally went for Theuma, Joseph Muscat’s administration crumbled.

Theuma had been warned of his planned arrest date but police swooped two days early, on 14 November 2019. Fenech had urged him in messages beforehand to dispose of the evidence. The jury saw one message in which he said: “Be 100% sure everywhere is clean.”

But Theuma held on to his recordings. On 19 November, the prime minister signed a memorandum guaranteeing Theuma immunity from prosecution in exchange for testimony. Within hours, Fenech was making preparations to flee, messages seen by the jury suggest. “Go while you’re still in time,” his uncle texted. He planned to sail to Sicily, and then head for France. However, the police had been tipped off. His yacht was intercepted a mile off the coast, and he was arrested. The interrogation tapes, played at his trial, showed he offered to implicate Schembri in return for a pardon.

blocks.caption: A mass in memory of Caruana Galizia in Valletta. Photograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: As Fenech talked, heads rolled. Schembri was arrested in relation to the suspected leaks, and resigned. The economy minister, a frequent subject of Caruana Galizia’s blog, suspended himself and Mizzi, by now reassigned from energy to tourism minister, quit, citing “political, extraordinary and general circumstances in the country”.
Public outrage brought hundreds on to the streets, filling the grand plaza outside the prime minister’s office, chanting: “Mafia, mafia”.

Fenech’s pardon request was rejected and on 30 November, he was charged. Two days later, Joseph Muscat resigned. Defiant to the end, he insisted: “This case cannot define everything that our country is.”

The saga is once again drawing attention from outside Malta. Shami Chakrabarti, the British Labour peer, has been appointed rapporteur of a Council of Europe investigation into the Maltese government’s response to the murder. Caruana Galizia’s family members intend to give evidence at the first hearing next week.

“The failure to ensure individual accountability for the murder risks perpetuating a culture of impunity,” Chakrabarti said on Thursday. “A culture where … those who try to shine a light in the darkness pay the ultimate price.”

blocks.text: TAGBILARAN CITY, Bohol — The municipal government of Bilar, Bohol, has suspended classes in kindergarten, elementary and secondary levels in public and private schools due to worsening air quality caused by haze from wildfires in Indonesia’s Kalimantan and Sumatra regions.
Mayor Norman Palacio issued a memorandum Thursday, Sept. 3, ordering the suspension effective immediately and until further notice.
Smoke and particulate matter are being carried by prevailing winds from Indonesia toward Bohol and other parts of the country, particularly the Visayas and Mindanao.
Palacio advised residents to remain indoors whenever possible and limit unnecessary outdoor activities as a precaution against unhealthy air quality.
School heads and concerned officials were directed to disseminate the memorandum and ensure its immediate implementation.
The public was urged to remain vigilant, prioritize health and safety, and monitor official announcements for updates on the class suspension. /das

articles.title: SC invites Ombudsman to file ‘proper complaint’ over CA rulings
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court (SC) has invited the Office of the Ombudsman to file a “proper complaint” following Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla’s statement on Thursday regarding the Court…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court (SC) has invited the Office of the Ombudsman to file a “proper complaint” following Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla’s statement on Thursday regarding the Court of Appeals (CA) decisions reversing cases dismissed by the anti-graft body.
Remulla, during the Senate finance committee’s deliberations on the Ombudsman’s proposed 2027 budget, raised the issue of alleged delays in the country’s justice system.
He said, “Many of those that we have dismissed in the Office of the Ombudsman institutionally, in many cases, we’re talking about many, many cases that were reversed by the Court of Appeals.”
The Ombudsman also mentioned that he had discussed the matter with Supreme Court Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen.
Following this, the SC said in a statement Thursday evening that it takes allegations pertaining to partiality, misconduct and corruption “seriously.”

“[The SC] acts on such allegations when proper complaints are filed, evidence is presented, and the judges or justices concerned are given the opportunity to respond,” SC spokesperson Atty. Camille Ting said.
But the spokesperson pointed out that the SC “cannot act on broad allegations against an entire appellate court based only on public statements.”

“We therefore invite the Ombudsman, or any concerned party, to file the proper complaint and submit supporting evidence. This will allow the Court to determine the facts and, when warranted, exercise its disciplinary authority,” she emphasized.
Ting pointed out that the SC upholds the public’s “right to freedom of expression,” including their right to criticize the courts and their decisions.

She specifically mentioned the high court’s recent ruling clearing political analyst and Inquirer columnist Richard Heydarian, Akbayan party-list Rep. Perci Cendaña and presidential anti-poverty czar Larry Gadon of indirect contempt.

The three became respondents in the indirect contempt petitions after criticizing the SC following the release of its 2025 decision dismissing the 2024 impeachment complaints against Vice President Sara Duterte.
“Despite the strong statements made against the Court concerning one of its rulings, the Court upheld the respondents’ freedom of speech and did not hold them in contempt,” the SC spokesperson said.

“The Court welcomes fair criticism. At the same time, serious accusations against judges and courts should be raised through the proper processes so they can be fairly investigated and resolved,” she added.
The Inquirer reached out to Remulla about the SC’s statement but he had not responded as of press time. /das

articles.title: Sister denies detained Ontario university student is Chinese spy
articles.summary: The sister of an Ontario university student arrested in an FBI counter-intelligence investigation has denied her brother is knowingly involved in espionage for Beijing. Weiheng Zeng, a Chinese…

image.caption: University of Waterloo student Weiheng Zeng was arrested at the U.S. border in Michigan in August and charged with making false statements, amid an FBI counter-intelligence investigation. (Instagram/Billy Zeng)

blocks.text: World

The sister of an Ontario university student arrested in an FBI counter-intelligence investigation has denied her brother is knowingly involved in espionage for Beijing. Weiheng Zeng, a Chinese citizen, was arrested while attempting to cross the U.S. border.
Weiheng Zeng charged amid FBI counter-intelligence probe
The sister of an Ontario university student arrested in an FBI counter-intelligence investigation has denied her brother is knowingly involved in espionage for Beijing.
"If my brother is a Chinese spy, then I'm Trump's father," Meixuan Wang wrote in a social media post on Wednesday.

Weiheng Zeng — a Chinese citizen born in 2004 and a student at the University of Waterloo — was arrested while attempting to cross the U.S. border from Windsor, Ont., last month and charged with making false statements. According to a criminal complaint, Zeng admitted to accepting paid "taskings" from an individual he believed to be associated with a Chinese security service.

The complaint, filed in U.S. District Court in Michigan, includes security camera images which appear to show a man climbing a forklift, trying to open a locked FedEx truck and taking photos from a parking lot at Chicago's O’Hare International Airport in April.
According to court documents, Zeng told investigators his unnamed contact directed him to photograph aircraft and tail numbers, in exchange for $20-30 US per picture.

The criminal complaint, signed by FBI special agent Robert Holbrook, also says Zeng recounted trespassing and taking pictures last year at a FedEx facility at Toronto's Pearson International Airport, at the request of the same, unidentified individual.
The allegations amount to "espionage-type activities," prosecutor Alyse Wu told the Detroit court.
Gina Balaya, a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney's Office, said in an email to CBC News the case is still under investigation.
Ontario university student suspected of spying in Canada, U.S. for China
Self-described 'photography lover'

On Zeng’s public Instagram page — where he goes by the first name Billy — he describes himself as a "photography lover" and says he expects to graduate from Waterloo’s global business and digital arts program in 2028.
His profile features pictures of planes, including Canadian military aircraft apparently photographed at an airshow in 2024.
Zeng’s Instagram page also includes photos taken on trips to Chicago, where his sister lives and works as an artist, according to her social media pages.

Wang, who also goes by the first name Jade, told the Globe and Mail her brother is obsessed with airplanes and has autism spectrum disorder. She said Zeng may not have realized the trouble he was in when he was questioned by U.S. border officers.
Wang declined CBC News's interview request.
Celeste Kinney, a court-appointed federal defender who appeared on Zeng’s behalf at a previous hearing, told CBC News on Thursday she is not representing him.
Zeng is scheduled to again appear in court next week. He remains in custody and did not request to be released on bond.
RCMP spokesperson Camille Boily-Lavoie said the Mounties are aware of the case, but declined to say whether they were involved in the FBI’s probe. CSIS referred questions to the RCMP.
"I feel, in a way, sorry for [Zeng]," Margaret McCuaig-Johnston, an Ottawa-based advisory board member at the China Strategic Risks Institute think-tank, said in an interview earlier this week.
"I'm sure he didn't realize when he was doing this what he was getting into."
She said China's Ministry of State Security routinely leans on students abroad to gather information and take photos that could prove useful to Beijing's spy agencies.

items: The Canadian suspected of spying on NATO was denied bail. Here's what comes next
4 ex-Western University students accused in London, Ont., explosives-making scheme face 19 new charges
Plane spotter or Chinese spy? Ontario university student suspected of espionage at airports

blocks.text: "They don't have to use their own people to find out this information, and so they have deniability," McCuaig-Johnston said.

An unnamed spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Ottawa said in a statement on Wednesday that Beijing "firmly opposes hyping up the so-called 'China spy threat' and baseless speculations and smears against China."

Michel Juneau-Katsuya, who served as chief of the Asia-Pacific unit for CSIS, said people who agree to be paid to carry out tasks for intelligence organizations are referred to in the industry as "co-optees."
"The question is, is [Zeng] a spy or is he somebody who was recruited to do a job for a spy?" Juneau-Katsuya said. "And it sounds like maybe he's the latter."
With files from Tahlia Sarv

articles.title: ‘Unmute the video’: Ridon hits ‘no smoking gun’ claim in Duterte trial
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — House of Representatives impeachment prosecutor Rep. Terry Ridon on Thursday pushed back against claims by Vice President Sara Duterte’s supporters that the prosecution has…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — House of Representatives impeachment prosecutor Rep. Terry Ridon on Thursday pushed back against claims by Vice President Sara Duterte’s supporters that the prosecution has failed to produce a “smoking gun” after 21 days of trial, telling them to “unmute the video” and listen to the evidence and testimony presented in court.

“Again, without violating the sub judice restriction, perhaps the video of Duterte supporters has been muted, right? You need to unmute the video so you can hear the details because a lot has already been mentioned,” Ridon said during a press briefing.fing.
“But my advice to them is, my friend, unmute the video,” he added.

The Bicol Saro Party-list lawmaker was responding to a question on whether the prosecution has a “smoking gun” to present in the remaining impeachment charges after Duterte’s supporters claimed none had emerged during the first 21 days of trial.
Ridon declined to characterize the weight of the evidence, citing the Senate impeachment court’s sub judice restrictions.
“I won’t say whether it is very serious or not serious because that would fall under the sub judice restriction,” he said.
But Ridon questioned what Duterte’s supporters would consider a “smoking gun” after weeks of testimony and documentary evidence presented before the impeachment court.
“Because that is what the public has already seen. So what other smoking gun are they talking about?” he said.

The prosecution has completed its presentation of evidence on the article involving Duterte’s alleged threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and then-Speaker Martin Romualdez.

It is currently presenting evidence on Article I involving the alleged misuse and irregular liquidation of P612.5 million in confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President and Department of Education.

Ridon said the prosecution believes the evidence it has presented on the first two articles it tackled is “more than sufficient,” while stressing that he would not discuss the weight of specific evidence because of the sub judice rule.

articles.title: Venezuelan opposition leader questions US oil deal with ‘illegitimate regime’
articles.summary:
María Corina Machado says interim government does not have democratic mandate to negotiate natural resources

The Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, has questioned Donald…

blocks.text: The Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, has questioned Donald Trump’s oil deal with Venezuela’s interim government, declaring that the country’s natural resources do not belong to “an illegitimate regime”.

In her first public comments since Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Venezuela last Friday, Machado walked a diplomatic tightrope between challenging the controversial agreement and trying not to rile the White House.

In a video posted on social media, the Nobel peace prize winner said: “Of course the United States is the principal partner Venezuela needs to fully develop its strategic potential. This is what the majority of Venezuelans believe … and it is something I’ve spent my whole life defending.”

However, Machado said the current occupants of the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas were “enemies of the US” and claimed they did not have the right or the democratic mandate to negotiate Venezuela’s natural resources. “The wealth of our subsoil does not belong to an illegitimate regime – it belongs to the Venezuelan people,” said Machado, recognising that supporters felt “sadness and anger” at being excluded from the decision-making process.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels – more than 65bn barrels of which are involved in the agreement.
Trump’s deal was struck with the un-elected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who took power in January after her strongman predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces.

Many observers expected Trump to replace Maduro with Machado, a conservative democracy activist who later gave the US president her Nobel prize award. But Trump instead backed Rodríguez, warning: “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price – probably bigger than Maduro.” Machado has been sidelined.

The White House claims the oil deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves.

Speaking outside the Miraflores palace on Wednesday, the US energy secretary, Chris Wright, said the aim was “to massively grow production and economic opportunities in Venezuela”. “President Trump has a clear mission in Venezuela. The mission is to bring peace, freedom, opportunity, and prosperity to everyone in Venezuela,” Wright told reporters.

But there has been widespread condemnation of what critics have called a predatory and colonial-style land grab. Machado’s supporters fear the deal makes Washington far less inclined to push for fresh presidential elections.

Machado’s movement is widely believed to have beaten Maduro by a landslide in the last such vote, in 2024, but he refused to accept the result and clung to power until his dramatic rendition on 3 January 2026.
On Wednesday, both Trump and Rodríguez brushed off questions about when an election might be held.
“You had a very powerful, very nasty dictatorship in Venezuela – and they’re just not going to be ready for it yet,” Trump told reporters, before adding vaguely: “But soon.”
Asked when an election would be held, Rodríguez said: “There will be an electoral process, but when Venezuela is ready.”
“I don’t set dates,” she added.

articles.title: Trump hints US would not back UK over Falkland Islands due to lack of Iran war support
articles.summary: The US president says the UK was not "there to help me" in his ongoing war with Iran.

blocks.text: Donald Trump has hinted he would not come to the UK's aid in a potential future conflict with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.
In an interview with GB News, the US president said that Britain had "not been there to help me" with his country's war with Iran, despite later saying his military did not need any support.
Trump's latest remarks come after he previously said the US could revise its neutral position on the islands' sovereignty if the UK failed to increase defence spending.
Argentinian President Javier Milei is due to make a televised statement on Thursday night about what he describes as his nation's "historic" claim to the islands.
The Falklands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina, more than 40 years on from an armed conflict over the territory.
When asked if he would "come to the UK's aid" during a potential territorial dispute, Trump told GB News: "Well look, I was there when they had the first war.
"That was a long time ago and I watched it so carefully, and you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly, but it's a long way away."

Turning his attention to the US' current conflict with Iran, he added: "So, your country's not doing well. Don't forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren't there to help me.
"Your country was not there to help me. We didn't need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, 'why didn't you send a couple of ships?'
Trump said the-then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, told him no vessels were available, which "was pretty sad", he added.
He also said: "Nato was not there, even though they get – most of those countries get – a big portion of their oil from there. So we're doing that by ourselves".
Argentina and the UK waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.
Seventy-four days of fighting led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.
Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.
Trump's comments come after he was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the islands.
The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."
The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".
A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."
In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.
