blocks.text: Bangladesh’s current government, headed by the center-right Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), is in favor of the Mecca agreement.
“We view this pact positively,” Bangladeshi Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman said in response to a question in parliament last week.
But he insisted that the question of Bangladesh joining the pact, or even considering membership, had not yet arisen, as that would depend on the intentions of its current members.
“If they express an intention to include Bangladesh in the pact, we will certainly consider it positively,” he said.
When asked about the remarks made by Bangladeshi officials, India said the pact had implications for its national security and that it was closely monitoring the situation.

“We continue to follow all developments that have a bearing on India’s security and take all necessary steps to safeguard it,” Randhir Jaiswal, a spokesperson for India’s Ministry of External Affairs, told reporters in New Delhi last week.
Competing geopolitical interests
Analysts said Dhaka needs to consider its interests carefully before making any move to join the joint defense pact.

“The scope for direct conventional interstate war or military conflict in South Asia is limited. Therefore, the primary role of such an agreement is not confined to conducting border wars,” said Murshid.
“In international relations, its significance lies mainly in strengthening bargaining power and maintaining one’s position against the influence of other regional countries.”
Murshid added that Pakistan’s interest in bringing Bangladesh closer through this agreement “is driven by geographical and political considerations.”

“For India, the security of the Siliguri Corridor and its eastern frontier are important considerations,” she said, referring to India’s narrow land link to its northeastern states, which wraps around Bangladesh to the north. “If Pakistan’s defense-related influence in Bangladesh were to increase, New Delhi could view this as a development capable of affecting the regional balance of relationships.”
In such circumstances, Bangladesh would have to clearly define what it would and would not do by joining this alliance, she explained.

“In particular, a clear position would be necessary regarding Bangladesh’s role if a military conflict were to arise between India and Pakistan. Taking Pakistan’s side during such a conflict could create political and diplomatic pressures for Dhaka that may exceed Bangladesh’s capacity to manage,” she stressed.

Dhaka-based former diplomat M Humayun Kabir sees no reason for Bangladesh to join the pact. “Bangladesh has not joined any military alliance over the past 50 to 55 years. As far as I am concerned, I believe that position remains unchanged to this day,” he told DW.

“They are talking about a regional security arrangement, but the region in question concerns Pakistan and the Middle East. We are not part of that region or geographical area. Bangladesh is located in the eastern part of South Asia. Therefore, there is no direct geographical rationale for Bangladesh to participate in such a military alliance,” he added.
Would Bangladesh benefit from joining the pact?
Murshid stressed that Bangladesh needed to develop its own defense infrastructure and security systems sustainably.
She believes that becoming part of an international security agreement could help modernize Dhaka’s defense capabilities and facilitate access to military technology.

“The text of the agreement does not directly mention trade, labor markets or economic relations. However, it is natural for economic elements to become linked with a security framework, a phenomenon known in international relations as issue linkage,” she said.

However, Kabir fears joining the pact could limit Bangladesh’s geopolitical options and recommended a balanced approach. “We contribute to peacekeeping missions around the world under the auspices of the United Nations, and that is important to us. Our economy is interconnected with many different countries in various ways, which is also important. Our workforce is present in countries across the world, and that, too, is an important consideration,” he said.
“Therefore, before making any decision on this issue, we must take into account the many different dimensions and forms of our national interests.” /dl

articles.title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find
articles.summary:
Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every…

blocks.text: Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.

Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.

Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.

blocks.caption: Young farm workers harvesting cotton in a field near Boromo in Burkina Faso. Photograph: Issouf Sanogo/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.

Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”

The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
after newsletter promotion

Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”

Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.

Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.

Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.

Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

articles.title: American, wife killed in Dumaguete City
articles.summary: BACOLOD CITY—The police are investigating the violent killing of an American national and his Filipino wife in Barangay Bajumpandan, Dumaguete City early on Wednesday. Capt. Stephen Polinar,…

blocks.text: BACOLOD CITY—The police are investigating the violent killing of an American national and his Filipino wife in Barangay Bajumpandan, Dumaguete City early on Wednesday.

Capt. Stephen Polinar, spokesperson for the Negros Oriental Police Provincial Office, said the victims were shot at around 4 a.m. and were officially reported to the Dumaguete City Police Station around 6:08 a.m. Both victims were residents of the barangay.
Preliminary findings reveal that two unidentified male assailants carried out the attack before quickly fleeing the scene.
The Dumaguete City Police Station has since identified a person of interest in connection with the case.

While the primary motive behind the attack remains undetermined, law enforcement teams are actively conducting follow-up operations and gathering evidence to track down and apprehend the perpetrators./coa

articles.title: Japan halves speed limit to 30km/h on all narrow city streets
articles.summary:
Speed limit dropped from 60km/h for around 70% of general roads in the hope of making narrow streets of crowded cities safer

Drivers on residential roads in

blocks.text: Drivers on residential roads in Japan have been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets.
The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said.

Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident.

The measures apply to about 870,000km of roads that are less than 5.5 metres wide and do not have centre lines or median strips, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said.
Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements in safety seen on larger roads.

While the overall number of deaths in traffic accidents is in decline – falling to a record low of 2,457 last year – those involving children and older people on residential roads has remained steady at about 300 a year since 2021, and rose for the first time in three years in 2025, according to the national police agency.
The introduction in 2011 of “zone 30” areas on a limited number of residential streets and along school routes resulted in a 30% reduction in fatalities and serious injuries, the Mainichi said.

Police agency data show that the mortality rate among pedestrians is less than 1% in accidents involving vehicles traveling at or below 30km/h, with the rate rising to 2.7% at speeds of 30-40km/h, and to 17.4% at 50-60km/h.

“We ask drivers to recognise that they need to take particular care on roads shared by vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists,” the police agency’s commissioner general, Yoshinobu Kusunoki, told reporters this week.

articles.title: This is not standard flooding; it is Himalayan tsunami – Nepal minister
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Following the unprecedented disaster in Rasuwa and surrounding northern districts, Nepal finds itself in the grip of a profound humanitarian and infrastructural crisis. Foreign…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Following the unprecedented disaster in Rasuwa and surrounding northern districts, Nepal finds itself in the grip of a profound humanitarian and infrastructural crisis. Foreign Affairs Minister Shisir Khanal speaks about the scale of the disaster, the logistical nightmare of high-altitude tunnel rescues, and why Nepal is shifting its diplomatic posture from requesting humanitarian aid to demanding climate compensation.
This Q&A has been edited for clarity and length, and is based on an interview on Kantipur TV’s Fireside by Rupesh Shrestha.
Minister, you recently returned from a field visit to Nuwakot. What is the real-world scale of this disaster?

When the first reports came in around 9am, our immediate conceptual imagery of a “flood” was a standard seasonal rise in river levels. But having spent the day in Nuwakot, I realized how limited our vocabulary is.

This was not a standard flood. With wave heights reaching 20 to 30 meters and speeds clocked at 180 kilometers per hour, this was a disaster of tornado-like velocity—what many are rightly calling a “Himalayan Tsunami”. It is a scale of disaster that is entirely outside the living memory of Nepal.

The damage is immense. Early assessments indicate that ten municipalities across Nuwakot, Rasuwa, and Dhading—spanning 30 to 32 wards—have been heavily impacted, with additional damage downstream in Gorkha and Chitwan. We are looking at tens of thousands of damaged private homes, alongside heavily hit schools and multi-billion-rupee hydropower projects.
There has been criticism that the government was slow to seek international help, choosing instead to rely on its own resources. How do you respond to this?

There was absolutely no delay or rigidity on our part. The disaster unfolded rapidly. By 11am, while the floodwaters were still surging toward Dhading, the prime minister convened the National Disaster Council and mobilized security forces for immediate search and rescue.

Our initial priority was saving lives on the surface. By the second day, as our ground teams assessed the buried hydropower projects, they reported a critical need for highly specialized tunnel rescue support. We communicated this need immediately.

Because of high-altitude weather and transport limitations, airlift was the only viable option. Despite heavy cloud cover on the third afternoon that delayed flights, the Indian specialized tunnel rescue team arrived on the ground by the evening of the third day. The Chinese specialized team arrived by the afternoon of the fourth day, and a South Korean team is actively working at the Upper Trishuli site. Within 72 hours of identifying the need, international specialized rescue operations were fully operational on-site.
What is the status of the rescue operations at the buried hydropower tunnels, such as Trishuli 3A and Chilime? Is there still hope of finding survivors?

We must maintain hope and exhaust every possibility. Historically, there are global precedents—such as the 2018 Thailand cave rescue, or tunnel incidents in India in 2023 and China in 2021—where survivors were rescued after 14 to 18 days due to natural air pockets. Even if a tunnel is partially blocked, if there are air pockets, survival is possible.

However, the public must understand the extreme complexity on the ground. This is a highly complex disaster. These are not simple horizontal cave openings. The entire topography has shifted; hillsides have sheared off, leaving vertical cliffs covered in deep, unstable debris. In some areas, our rescue teams are literally sinking into quicksand-like mud.

At Trishuli 3A, teams had to locate the buried tunnel entrance using engineered maps because the surface construction was entirely erased. Instead of drilling horizontally, rescuers had to dig a vertical shaft—like a 30-foot well—just to reach the concrete crown of the tunnel. Once they breached it, they immediately began pumping in oxygen.

Currently, the Chinese team is working at the Trishuli 3A site, the Indian teams are deployed at Chilime and Langtang, and the South Korean team is coordinating at Upper Trishuli. While our security forces successfully cleared and entered the final points of the Rasuwagadhi tunnel on Monday, unfortunately, no survivors or bodies were recovered there. We are continuing to mobilise every local and international resource available.

The Rasuwagadhi-Kerung border is closed, and there are reports of temporary closures at Tatopani. How is the government managing bilateral trade and stranded travellers, particularly Mansarovar pilgrims?

Our northern supply chains and tourist corridors have been severely disrupted. Because the Tibet Autonomous Region is highly sensitive, Chinese regulations typically dictate that travelers must exit through the exact border post they entered.

To bypass this restriction, we actively negotiated with Chinese authorities to allow stranded Nepalis and foreign tourists to exit via alternative crossings. Stranded Nepalis have already begun returning through the Hilsa crossing in Humla. Furthermore, we have formally requested that the Korola border crossing in Mustang be used to evacuate foreign tourists who cannot return via Rasuwagadhi.

Regarding trade, hundreds of cargo trucks are currently stranded on the Chinese side of the Rasuwagadhi border. We have requested permission from Chinese authorities to reroute these cargo flows through the Tatopani and Korola crossings to prevent a total collapse of our northern supply lines.
You have stated that Nepal will no longer treat post-disaster assistance as mere “humanitarian aid” or bilateral grants. What is the government’s new diplomatic strategy?

Nepal’s greenhouse gas emissions are virtually negligible. Yet, we are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create. The rapid melting of glaciers and these catastrophic mountain tsunamis are direct consequences of global climate change.

We are shifting our diplomatic framework from “aid” to “justice and compensation”. This is not a matter of charity; it is a matter of legal and moral liability. The major industrial emitters—such as China, which is the world’s top emitter, the United States at number two, and India at number three—have a historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal.

To this end, the Ministry of Finance has officially dispatched a formal climate compensation claim letter to our international partners. We will be raising this issue with absolute firmness and clarity at every upcoming international forum. This is a matter of civilizational survival. If our Himalayan glaciers disappear, the water security of over two billion people in South Asia—dependent on rivers like the Ganges and the Trishuli—will be permanently compromised. We are advocating not just for Nepal, but for the survival of South Asian civilization.

There is a strong perception that the government is more active on social media than on the ground, and that citizen deaths are treated merely as statistics. Why does Prime Minister Balendra Shah use his personal Facebook page to disseminate official government updates instead of official institutional channels? What about citizens who are not on social media, or cannot read?

For those whose family members are still missing or out of contact, their grief and frustration are completely understandable, and the government’s sole objective is to mobilize every available resource to find them. A citizen’s life is never just a number to us; it represents a family’s entire future, hope, and happiness.

Regarding the prime minister’s communications, his personal Facebook page has been his primary political platform since the very beginning of his public career. It has millions of followers, making it mathematically the most immediate and effective channel to reach a massive audience. While the Prime Minister’s Office maintains its own official communication handles, the reach on his personal page is far greater. These updates are immediately picked up by mainstream newspapers, television networks, and radio stations. This broadcast ensures that regular video and audio reports are generated, effectively reaching citizens who are not on social media or are illiterate.

Many citizens stranded in temporary camps, such as Laharepauwa, complain that while they see helicopters flying overhead, actual relief supplies—food, clothing, and sanitary products—are not reaching them. How is the government regulating relief distribution?

We recognize these grievances and are working to streamline the supply chain. In the initial rescue phase, helicopter flights are centralized and highly fluid—sometimes flying to extract a single stranded individual, which is highly inefficient from a resource perspective but necessary to save lives.

For the relief phase, we have established a strict coordination mechanism. Relief materials are dispatched only after direct coordination with local Ward Presidents to ensure they go where they are actually needed.

Regarding financial transparency, the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund has already received over Rs5 billion in public and diaspora contributions. This fund is heavily regulated and will be strictly channelled into immediate relief operations and long-term reconstruction. We are fully committed to ensuring that not a single rupee of these public donations is wasted on unnecessary administrative overheads or government luxury travel. We will stand firmly with our citizens through the rescue, relief, and eventual reconstruction phases. /dl

articles.title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in second national security case
articles.summary:
Wong, 29, is accused of urging foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades and other hostile measures against China

Joshua…

blocks.text: Joshua Wong, one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence.
Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions against Hong Kong and China.
The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong and China after the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts.
Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.
In 2022 he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. In November 2024 he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison.
Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock. He wore a blue shirt and black-rimmed glasses. He stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty to the charges.

Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be “of a grave nature”. Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence.
Outside Hong Kong’s high court, people queued overnight to secure a seat at Wednesday’s hearing.

blocks.caption: Hong Kong activist and supporters hold signs during a press event to support pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong in Taipei, Taiwan, on Wednesday. Photograph: Chiang Ying-ying/AP

blocks.text: In 2014, the then teenage Wong became the international face of the Umbrella Movement, when thousands of protesters occupied major roads across Hong Kong for 79 days demanding greater democracy. In October 2014 he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the movement and immediately joined calls for the bill to be withdrawn.

In 2020 Beijing imposed a wide-ranging national security law on Hong Kong after a year of anti-government protests. The authorities said the law was needed to restore stability to the international financial hub. Critics say six years on the law is continuing to expand in scope.

Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law. Supporters say the prosecution heavily relied on his advocacy before the national security law was enacted and argue his case has been applied retroactively.

“It’s obvious that the government wants to keep him behind bars for as long as they can, so as to isolate him and not to let him become a visible symbol of resistance.” said Frances Hui from the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation.
Wong’s case has attracted widespread condemnation from global rights organisations.

“By stacking one charge after another against Joshua Wong, the authorities are ensuring that the democracy icon stays behind bars, silencing him and the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement he helped lead and inspire,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.

“Conflating promoting democracy and free speech with undermining national security is a favourite dodge for authoritarians. Beijing also likes blaming ‘hostile’, but unspecified foreign forces,” said Sophie Richardson, a longtime China rights advocate.
On Tuesday the former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith urged the UK government to raise Wong’s case with Beijing, saying: “Enough is enough. It’s time to stop chasing peaceful protesters.”
With Associated Press

articles.title: Nepal seeks urgent climate finance after Bhotekoshi flood
articles.summary: The government has sent an urgent request to the board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, a global climate finance mechanism, seeking financial assistance for Nepal following the deadly…

blocks.text: The government has sent an urgent request to the board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, a global climate finance mechanism, seeking financial assistance for Nepal following the deadly Bhotekoshi flood of August 26.

The mechanism was established at COP27 in 2022 and operationalised at COP28. A letter cosigned by Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Forests and Agriculture Minister Geeta Chaudhary, a copy of which has been seen by the Post, seeks an immediate response to the catastrophic flash flood.

“We write to draw your urgent attention to the catastrophic flash flood that struck the Bhotekoshi river basin, causing widespread loss of life, displacement, destruction of homes and critical infrastructure, and severe disruption to essential services, livelihoods, markets, and connectivity across downstream communities,” the letter reads.

Maheshwar Dhakal, joint secretary at the Ministry of Forests and a member of the fund’s board, told the Post that the letter does not specify the actual scale of the losses and that it is up to the board to decide on financial assistance.
“Almost all major donors and global development partners are members of the board, and Nepal’s claims and potential risks are well-established, so the board must compensate us,” he said.

The disaster has affected a fragile transboundary mountain river system and generated cascading consequences extending far beyond the immediate flood zone, according to the letter. Search, rescue, relief and rapid damage-assessment operations are continuing, it says.

“The full scale of economic and non-economic loss and damage has yet to be determined; however, preliminary information indicates that the consequences are extensive and exceed Nepal’s immediate response capacity,” the letter reads.

If Nepal is able to secure support from the fund, it would set an example for other vulnerable countries, Dhakal said. The scale of damage caused by the flood, and the search, rescue, relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction required in its aftermath, has become a major challenge for Nepal, he said.

“Since we are genuinely suffering from the adverse effects of climate change, we have approached the board. The next board meeting is expected to convene on December 10, but we want to get an immediate response and support before that,” he told the Post, noting that this is the first time Nepal has sought support from the entity.

As a least developed and highly climate-vulnerable mountainous country, Nepal contributes negligibly to global greenhouse gas emissions yet continues to bear disproportionate and escalating climate impacts, the letter says.

It adds that the Bhotekoshi disaster demonstrates how extreme events in the cryosphere can rapidly cascade from high mountains to densely populated downstream areas, undermining development gains and affecting water, food, energy, health, infrastructure, ecosystems and human security.

“In view of the exceptional urgency and magnitude of this disaster, the Government of Nepal respectfully requests the Board to take a special decision to respond rapidly, directly, and effectively in accordance with its Governing Instrument,” the letter says.

“Time is of the essence,” it adds. “A prompt response would help protect affected populations, restore essential services, prevent further suffering and demonstrate that the fund can translate international solidarity into timely support for vulnerable countries and communities when it is most urgently needed.”

During an interview with Kantipur Television on Monday, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said Nepal would raise the flood and its impacts with the international community. He said a letter had already been sent to the board on Monday through the Ministry of Finance.

In December 2024, Nepal drew the attention of the International Court of Justice to the impacts of climate change, making a strong plea for climate justice to alleviate the suffering of Nepali citizens.

Making a presentation to the court’s public hearings on the “Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change”, then Foreign Minister Arzu Rana Deuba said global warming and consequent climate change increasingly threaten Nepal’s snow-capped mountains and glaciers. /dl

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln arrives at Thai port after gruelling 270 days at sea
articles.summary:
Ship has been plagued by reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health because of lengthy deployment

The USS Abraham Lincoln, an US aircraft carrier at the centre of a…
articles.byline: Natasha May in Pattaya, and agencies

blocks.text: The USS Abraham Lincoln, an US aircraft carrier at the centre of a row over conditions on board after months at sea as part of Donald Trump’s war against Iran, has arrived off a Thai port.

Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on the vessel, including attempted suicides, have made headlines around the world, provoking criticism of the president’s actions in the Middle East.

A heavy security presence was in force at Laem Chabang port near Pattaya, south of Bangkok, where the 5,000-strong crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln arrived on Wednesday morning after more than 270 days at sea.
The huge nuclear-powered ship left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.
The Lincoln left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.
The resort city of Pattaya, a rest-and-recreation destination for US troops since the Vietnam war, has stepped up security as it prepares to welcome the sailors and Marines.

blocks.caption: A tug boat greets the USS Abraham Lincoln as it arrives at the port in Laem Chabang, Chonburi, Thailand. Photograph: Sakchai Lalit/AP

blocks.text: The sailors will disembark in groups of approximately 50, according to police colonel Anek Srathongyoo, a superintendent of Pattaya city police station.

Once a quiet fishing village, Pattaya was transformed into one of the most infamous red light districts in the world with the arrival of American troops using military bases in Thailand during the Vietnam war.
At its peak, tens of thousands of US military personnel came through each year, said Pipatpong Fakfare, an associate professor specialising in tourism at Bangkok University.

“In my opinion, it’s really the founding influence for the town. The US military turned a quiet fishing village into a global destination for an international nightlife and entertainment hub in about 15 years,” he said.
Pattaya is now hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism.

Although the American troops left by the mid-70s, the sex industry infrastructure continued to grow, with European tourists taking their place, and more recently waves of Chinese and Russian visitors, Pipatpong said.

blocks.caption: The USS Abraham Lincoln has 5,000 sailors aboard. Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Sex work is illegal in Thailand, but authorities often turn a blind eye, said Pattarachit Gozzoli, a sociologist at Mahidol University in Bangkok.

Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, has downplayed the city’s past, saying there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied it was linked to the US arrivals. Local police arrested 25 women for soliciting on the beachfront promenade a week before the ship arrived.
The mayor said buses had been arranged to transport the sailors between the ship and Pattaya until the carrier departs on Sunday.
Outside one bar, a sign said: “Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service.”
Poramase said in a Facebook post: “They come to relax. Our preparations will focus on safety and ensuring fair pricing, so we don’t take advantage of them.”

He said they had been banned from water sports such as jetskis, and from taking advantage of Thailand’s lax cannabis laws, but encouraged them to enjoy the city’s many other attractions, from malls to religious sites.

articles.title: They survived the flood. Their families did not.
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — When the flood came, Purna Bahadur Ghale had seconds to decide whether to run. The 43-year-old executive member of Uttargaya Rural Municipality was in Shanti Bazar when the…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — When the flood came, Purna Bahadur Ghale had seconds to decide whether to run.

The 43-year-old executive member of Uttargaya Rural Municipality was in Shanti Bazar when the Bhotekoshi river burst through settlements in Rasuwa on August 26. Someone shouted that everyone should flee.
He ran towards his home in Khalte.
Shanti Bazar is about three kilometres from the village. But by the time Ghale reached Pahirebesi, the flood had already arrived. He barely escaped with his life.
“Seconds made the difference between life and death,” he said.
Now sheltering at the holding centre set up at Shivalaya Basic School in Laharepauwa, Ghale is struggling to comprehend what happened next. Seven members of his family are missing.
“I know neither whether they are alive nor where their bodies are,” he said. “Seven of my relatives were caught in the flood.”

Ghale fled uphill into the forest and spent two days there. On the third day, Friday, a Nepali Army helicopter rescued him and flew him to Bidur in neighbouring Nuwakot. On Sunday, he made the five-hour journey back to Uttargaya.
“Ward 1 has suffered the greatest damage,” he said. “The very people who were telling others to run to safety were themselves swept away.”

The villages of Khalte, Gogane, Tiru and Karmarang have suffered extensive human and property losses. Bodies have begun appearing along the riverbanks, many so badly damaged that they are difficult to identify.

Among Ghale’s missing relatives are his 75-year-old father Subba Ghale; his 16-year-old younger son Krishna Ghale; his elder son’s 24-year-old wife Suchita; his brother Bam Bahadur’s 24-year-old wife Som Maya; their daughters, five-year-old Binusa and three-year-old Sunita; and his 10-year-old nephew Bikram Tamang.
The homes of the two brothers stood close to each other. His brother also ran a grocery shop in the village. According to Ghale, the flood reached Khalte at around 9:30am.
“I escaped the flood. When I first heard that it was coming, I called home and told everyone to run,” he said. “I rushed home to save my family, but I never made it there.”
From a safer location, he repeatedly tried calling home. At first, no one answered. Eventually, the phones went dead.
“I haven’t slept because I don’t know what happened to my family,” he said. Within moments, the settlement had been reduced to a barren riverbed.
“There was no way to get home. The roads were gone,” he said. At the time, he did not even know who among his family members had survived.
It was only after reaching Laharepauwa on Saturday that he began learning how many of his relatives had been caught in the flood.
“What can I say? I have nothing to say,” Ghale said, tears filling his eyes. “My mind is simply not working.”
Despite his own loss, Ghale was busy compiling details of those missing because of his role as a member of the rural municipality executive. By Sunday, he had counted 54 missing people.
There were 257 houses in Khalte. “Not a single house is intact,” he said. Ghale and many others in the settlement had already survived one disaster.

“We were victims of the 2015 earthquake. We survived then,” he said. “I must have gone to Singha Durbar more than a hundred times to ask the federal government to move us somewhere safer. They always said they would, but they never did.”
The families had been displaced from Gogane by the earthquake and resettled in Khalte. Now, Ghale says, the government must provide survivors with safe housing and food.
Twenty-six-year-old Ranjina Tamang is also sheltering at Shivalaya Basic School in Laharepauwa with her four-month-old son.
She survived the flood. So did four children who were with her. Ranjina was serving food at home when the flood came down the Bhotekoshi river.
She had fed her seven-year-old daughter and was getting the child ready for school. She was also preparing to eat before accompanying her daughter to Uttargaya School.
Then she heard it. A deafening roar. A wall of water carrying a dark mass of debris.
Panic set in.

She lifted her four-month-old baby onto her back. With her left hand, she held her seven-year-old son Arjan. With her right, she grabbed Smriti, her five-year-old niece. She pushed eight-year-old Nandika, another of her nieces, ahead of her, urging her to move faster.
“I ran into the forest with them,” Ranjina said. “The flood had already reached us. I was almost unconscious, but I somehow managed to save everyone.”
She feared throughout the climb that the baby strapped to her back might have fallen. “I was terrified that my son might have slipped off without me realising it,” she said.
None of them had shoes on their feet. Ranjina suffers from asthma, and running uphill made it even harder to breathe.
She first reached Gerkhu village and the following day walked for hours before arriving at Shivalaya Basic School in Rasuwa.
By then, she still had no idea who had survived and who had been swept away.
Her father, Som Bahadur Tamang, who worked at the Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project, is among those missing. Her mother, Phul Maya, has collapsed from the shock and is staying in Dandagaun in Rasuwa.
“I haven’t even been able to speak to my mother properly on the phone,” Ranjina said. “There is no electricity here, and we cannot even charge our phones.”
Three of her uncles, Man Bahadur, Mangale and Urla Tamang, are also missing. They worked as labourers at different hydropower projects under construction in Rasuwa.

Five members of her maternal uncle’s family remain out of contact as well. “I have no clothes to wear. I have asthma and no medicine. I have a cold, and my baby has a fever,” she said. “Many people here are sick.”
Tarali Maya Tamang, another resident of Khalte, is living at the same holding centre.
Her eight-year-old daughter Sunita, 12-year-old son Samir, mother-in-law Lenchon and father-in-law Mingmar Ghale are all missing.
“My children were swept away on their way to school,” she said. “My in-laws were at home when the flood suddenly came and took them.”

Her elder son Ramesh survived by running to safety. Tarali Maya herself was in Khalte when the flood struck and fled into the forest. Her husband, Temba, and elder daughter, Sushina, who were in Gogane at the time, also managed to escape to safety.
“Where do we go now? What are we going to eat? We don’t know anything,” she said, breaking down. “My family is gone. My home is gone. We have no food, no clothes, nothing.”
For Buddhi Bahadur Tamang, the disaster took his wife.

The Khalte resident, who is deaf and makes a living as a daily wage labourer, was outside his home when the flood came. He saw the water and ran. He survived, but his 43-year-old wife, Rata Kumari, could not.
His son works abroad. Because Buddhi Bahadur cannot hear, he has been unable to speak to his son on the phone. He, too, is now staying at the holding centre in Laharepauwa.
Twenty-seven-year-old Bam Bahadur Ghale lost almost everyone closest to him. His wife Som Maya and their daughters, Binusa and Sunita, were swept away.
“Now there is no one left in my family,” he said through tears. “I have nowhere to go. There is no home, no village, no relatives. We haven’t even found the bodies of our loved ones.”
He survived because he was away from home when the flood struck.
“Now I regret not being at home,” he said. “Sometimes I think that if I had gone with my family, at least I would not have to live like this, with nothing and no one.”
Survivors in the village are now struggling even with basic necessities. Many people have been crammed into a single room. New mothers have not been receiving adequate nutritious food.
Forty-two-year-old Chhegu Lama had survived the 2015 earthquake. After the disaster, he and his family had moved to the Khalte riverbed settlement. This time, he lost several members of his family.
His sister Kaisang Buti, two brothers-in-law, his father Sonam, mother Yosong Maya, younger brother Ujjen Singh Tamang and nephew Dinesh are all missing.

“After the earthquake, the government told us this was not a suitable place to live and promised to move us somewhere safer,” Lama said. “But we continued living here, and now the flood has taken everything too. There is hardly anyone left in the village. What a disaster this has been.”
He is also staying at the holding centre in Laharepauwa. The full scale of the destruction is still unclear.

According to Bishwas Nepali, a resident of nearby Kalika Rural Municipality-3 and a social activist involved in relief and rehabilitation efforts, preliminary estimates suggest that around 1,000 households across different wards of Uttargaya Rural Municipality have been affected.

“I am from this area, so we are involved in rescue, relief and rehabilitation efforts and helping in whatever way we can,” he said. “But we have not yet been able to collect complete data on the number of people affected.”

Local units and civil society groups are still compiling the figures. Many survivors escaped with nothing. “They have no clothes to wear. Children have no books or exercise copies to study with,” Nepali said.

Schools are currently being used as temporary shelters, and relief supplies have only recently begun arriving. “Representatives of the rural municipality are still occupied with rescue work and managing bodies,” he said.
According to Nepali, three areas in Uttargaya have been particularly hard hit: Mailung in ward 1, Pahirebesi in ward 4 and Khalte in ward 5.
He said government relief had yet to reach some of the affected settlements, while supplies brought by organisations and individuals were being stored and distributed through the local government.
There are currently five holding centres in the area, with students, elderly people, women and men accommodated separately.
“This arrangement may work for a short time,” Nepali said. “But if people have to stay like this for too long, health problems will emerge.” The next step, he said, must be temporary resettlement.

articles.title: Norway’s King Haakon VIII swears allegiance to constitution
articles.summary: OSLO — Norway’s King Haakon VIII took an oath before parliament on Tuesday, the first major institutional step of his reign, though his wife, still convalescing after a lung transplant,…

blocks.text: OSLO — Norway’s King Haakon VIII took an oath before parliament on Tuesday, the first major institutional step of his reign, though his wife, still convalescing after a lung transplant, was unable to attend.

Dressed in a ceremonial uniform, the 53-year-old Haakon, who became king when his father King Harald V died on Friday morning aged 89, swore to abide by the Scandinavian country’s constitution, under which the royals have a primarily symbolic function.
“I promise and swear that I will govern the Kingdom of Norway in accordance with its Constitution and Laws, so help me God, the almighty and omniscient,” he recited in the parliament’s main chamber.
Haakon’s wife Queen Mette-Marit, 53, was not beside her husband as she is still recovering from her June 17 transplant.

Media photographs showed her hours after the ceremony arriving at hospital in a car driven by the king himself. They showed him then leaving the facility without her and later returning to pick her up.
Are Holm, head of the Pulmonary Department at Oslo University Hospital, said in a statement from the palace that complications after a transplant are not “uncommon”.
“The queen has had complications on several occasions since the operation, including today,” Holm said.
“As a result, the queen must be kept under observation throughout the day,” he continued.
Moment of silence
The couple’s eldest daughter, Ingrid Alexandra, now crown princess at 22, attended her father’s ceremony.
She also took the oath Tuesday, but in writing at the Royal Palace.
Haakon and the members of parliament also observed a minute of silence in tribute to Harald.
Harald’s funeral will be held on September 9 at Oslo Cathedral. He will then be laid to rest in the royal mausoleum at Akershus Fortress in the Norwegian capital.
On Tuesday, thousands lined up outside the Royal Palace’s chapel where Harald is lying in state and will do so until the day before the funeral.
The king died while being treated at Oslo University Hospital for hemolytic anemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells.
He faced mounting health problems in his final years, forcing him to scale back his official schedule, but always ruled out abdicating.
Growing support
Harald, widely seen as the embodiment of an open and tolerant Norway, enjoyed massive support despite the scandals that dogged his family in the final stretch of his 35-year reign.
On Tuesday, a poll published by public broadcaster NRK showed that support for the monarchy had clearly increased following Harald’s death.

Nearly three out of four Norwegians, or 72 percent, said they supported the monarchy, a rise of eight points compared with a previous survey in May, according to the poll carried out over the weekend.
Support for the monarchy had fallen to its lowest level in February — though 60 percent were still in favour — while the royal family was mired in a series of scandals.
In particular, Mette-Marit faced scrutiny for her ties to late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
And her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, is currently under house arrest pending his appeal against a four-year sentence for two rape convictions.
The 29-year-old was able to visit Harald in hospital on the eve of his death and on Monday he was among those who brought the late king’s casket to the palace chapel.
He has also been granted permission to attend the funeral.

In the NRK survey, members of the royal family — of which Hoiby is not formally part — were also evaluated. Mette-Marit received one of the lowest character scores of 5.2 out of 10, compared to Haakon’s 8.8.
King Haakon and his wife will not be crowned, as Norway abolished coronations in 1908.
But, like his father and grandfather before him, Haakon could opt for a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral, where Norwegian monarchs were crowned between 1814 and 1906. /dl

articles.title: Relief as five Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet flood disaster found alive
articles.summary: Several missing Australians have been found since Tuesday morning, bringing the total citizens unaccounted for to 38

blocks.text: A total of five Australians missing after devastating floods ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border last week have been found.
Of the five Australians confirmed safe, one was found in Nepal, one in Tibet, and three outside the crisis-hit area. The total number still missing is 38.
These Australians had not spoken to families and next of kin since the disaster struck seven days ago.
There were “grave concerns” for the dozens of citizens still missing in the disaster, the minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, told the ABC on Wednesday morning.
“There are real logistic issues, including communications to find out where people are,” she said.

“For those families that are still waiting, those 38 individuals unaccounted for, we understand that it’s a really concerning time, and we’ll continue to do what we can to try and locate those people.”
Earlier, the minister for the Pacific, Pat Conroy, told Radio National the government was “focused on establishing their whereabouts and supporting their families”.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) has received nearly 800 calls in relation to the floods, with 18 Australian personnel having travelled to Nepal to join staff on the ground.
More humanitarian and disaster relief from Australia was due to arrive in Nepal on Wednesday afternoon.
Another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino, was safely located last week.
After an Australian in Tibet made contact with family and Dfat yesterday, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said the government was “incredibly thankful”.
“It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.”
The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet.
More than 4,400 people are missing.
Wong said the government needed to “remain realistic” about the days ahead.
“Communications remain difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed and many areas are still difficult to reach,” she said.
“As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted for inevitably grow.
“Our thoughts remain firmly with all those waiting for news of family and friends, and with the search and rescue teams working in extraordinarily difficult circumstances.”
Australia has sent a $8m assistance package for affected communities on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet.
Nepal has deployed nearly 20,000 security personnel to support search and rescue, and Chinese state media has reported that 2,141 emergency personnel have been deployed.

articles.title: Briton among 119 more people rescued in Nepal after flash floods
articles.summary:
More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000 still missing in disaster triggered by glacial collapse

A British national was among 119 people rescued in Nepal on Tuesday, an…

blocks.text: A British national was among 119 people rescued in Nepal on Tuesday, an official said almost a week after deadly flash floods on the country’s border with Tibet.
An army spokesperson told reporters at a press conference that Tuesday’s rescue efforts had saved 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men.
“We have also rescued one British male during this search and rescue operation, and the search and rescue operation is continuing,” he said.
The British man is yet to be identified. The UK Foreign Office was contacted for comment.
The rescues mark a rare breakthrough in a devastating week for Himalayan communities on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border.
At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing.
Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday.
Preliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster.

The collapse – so large it was initially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake – triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday.
Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris.
Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stations in the region.
“Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday.
Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33.

A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts.
The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster.
Scientists have said such disasters are more likely as the climate crisis affects mountainous and polar regions.
The UN’s top scientific advisory body said in 2023 that previously ice-bound landmasses – such as permafrost tundra and mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose.
Officials from Nepal, China and Tibet met in May to discuss strengthening their joint response to floods, weather and glacier-related hazards, Reuters reported on Tuesday.

articles.title: 'Tapusin na yan!': Prosecution to finish confidential funds article next week, says Chua
articles.summary: Saying they don't want an overly lengthy impeachment trial, members of the House prosecution panel intend to conclude its presentation on the confidential funds misuse article against Vice President…

blocks.text: Saying they don't want an overly lengthy impeachment trial, members of the House prosecution panel intend to conclude its presentation on the confidential funds misuse article against Vice President Sara Duterte next week.
According to solon-prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, the team is already looking to shift to the two remaining articles of impeachment.

“Masasabi natin, baka by next week ay matapos na, hopefully, ang confidential funds, and we will move on to the next article,” Chua said Tuesday afternoon, Sept. 1 during the prosecution's post-hearing press conference.
(We can say that, hopefully, we could finish the confidential funds article by next week, and we will move on to the next article.)

On Tuesday, Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Colonels Manaros Boransing II and Magtanggol Panopio testified about Army certifications that were used in the Department of Education’s (DepEd) response to state auditors.

In an effort to shorten its witness list, Chua said two other military officers would no longer be presented since their expected testimony would largely repeat the points already placed on the record.
“Iisa lang naman iyong sasabihin nila. To shorten—ayaw naman natin ng protracted hearing. Gusto natin matapos na rin ito.”
(They would only be saying the same thing. To shorten [the proceedings]—we don’t want a protracted hearing. We also want this to be finished.)
Chua said prosecutors already covered the central points involving the Youth Leadership Summits (YLS) and the military certifications.

Respondent Duterte is being accused--among other things--of misuing a total of P612.5 million worth of confidential funds released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and Department of Education (DepEd).
On Wednesday, Sept. 2, the prosecution expects to present former DepEd undersecretary and chief-of-staff Michael Wesley Poa, as well as a representative of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA)

Poa, currently Duterte’s defense lawyer, is expected to address the chain behind the military certifications, while the PSA witness will cover its checks of names appearing in confidential-fund records.

After those witnesses, the Manila solon said the remaining article I lineup would be short. “Ang natitira na lamang si Mr. Edward Fajarda, and probably isa—or at most, dalawa,” he said, referring to DepEd’s former special disbursing officer (SDO).
“The only one remaining is Mr. Edward Fajarda, and probably one—or at most, two [more witnesses].”
He said the prosecution will make its final lineup decision after Wednesday’s hearing. The panel previously finished its presentation of evidence on article IV, or the death threats article.
Defense's turn next
Chua reminded impeachment trial watchers that once the prosecution finishes all four articles of impeachment, the defense must present its own case.
“May target kasi tayo. We have to understand, after us mayroon pang defense; sila naman ang magpe-present. Siyempre ayaw naman natin na umabot pa ito by next year,” he said.
(We have a target. We have to understand that after us, there is still the defense; they will be the ones to present [their case]. Of course, we don’t want this to extend into next year.)

"Sana, hopefully, by November tapos na lahat (Hopefully, everything will be finished by November), so by December we can have the decision of the impeachment court whether or not to convict the Vice President," Chua said.

articles.title: Will impeachment trial prosecutors resign? Not anymore, says Chua
articles.summary: The House prosecution team's core of 11 solon-prosecutors will remain intact in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial. Thus, said prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, with the…

blocks.text: The House prosecution team's core of 11 solon-prosecutors will remain intact in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial.
Thus, said prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, with the revelation shelving a proposal for some of them to resign from the panel so they could speak publicly about the merits of the case.
“We have decided, wala na lang munang mag-resign,” Chua said Tuesday, Sept. 1 following day 20 of the high-stakes proceedings.
The panel considered a reshuffle after the Senate impeachment court reiterated the sub judice rule, or the limits on public comments about matters being tried.

One option was for selected House prosecutors to leave the panel and serve only as spokespersons. “Noong una, isa iyon sa mga naging discussion kung ganoon ang mangyayari. Kasi iyon ang talagang unang option,” Chua said.
(At first, that was one of the discussions, if that was what would happen. Because that was really the first option.)
The idea drew support from lawyers working with the team. “May mga suggestion ang ibang private prosecutor at public prosecutor na may ilan mag-resign para maging spokesperson."
(Some private prosecutors and public prosecutors suggested that some members resign so they could serve as spokespersons.)
But Chua said the prosecution members ultimately chose continuity. He noted that changing the structure of the team at this stage would require finding replacements.
“After considering everything, total isang buwan na lang kung masusunod iyong ating target...Too late na kung magbabawas tayo at magdadagdag pa,” Chua said.
(After considering everything, there’s only about a month left if we follow our target...It’s too late if we start removing and adding members.)
As such, the team will keep public briefings focused on schedules, witness sequencing, and other procedural updates.
More importantly, Chua said the prosectors "will just try to explain things in a way that does not touch on the merits [of the case]".

That was also why Chua, a public prosecutor, appeared at Tuesday’s briefing. He said reporters could still ask about what comes next without forcing prosecutors into a public discussion of the evidence.
“Baka may magtanong tungkol sa procedural aspect outside the merits of the case, so I can answer that,” said the veteran lawmaker from Manila.
(Someone might ask about the procedural aspects outside the merits of the case, so I can answer that.)
The approach allows the public to receive practical updates while the same prosecutors continue their work inside the impeachment court, Chua said.
It also preserves the team’s current assignments as the prosecution tries to finish article I on confidential funds and move to the remaining articles of impeachment against Duterte.
Fifteen private prosecutors are helping the solon-prosecutors gain a conviction from the respondent, free of charge.

articles.title: Philippines prepares for unprecedented 5-million tons rice imports
articles.summary: The Philippines will import a record-high five million metric tons (MT) this year, as it turns to foreign supplies to offset a projected shortfall in domestic production caused by El Niño, according…

blocks.text: The Philippines will import a record-high five million metric tons (MT) this year, as it turns to foreign supplies to offset a projected shortfall in domestic production caused by El Niño, according to the Department of Agriculture (DA).

“As we are facing El Niño, we are projecting that we might need to import up to five million MT for this year,” said Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel during his agency’s budget hearing on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The projected import volume this year is nearly four percent higher than the current record of 4.81 million MT set in 2024.
Total rice imports as of Aug. 13 reached 3.46 million MT, already higher than the 3.39 million MT recorded last year, according to the Bureau of Plant Industry (BPI).
Tiu Laurel said the additional rice supply will serve as a buffer as the country’s rice production losses are estimated to reach 900,000 MT within the year.
He said the decline represents the “worst-case scenario” of a strong El Niño in the fourth quarter of the year, which is projected to damage several hectares of rice farms.
“What we are all doing this year is precautionary. It is better to be prepared and have enough supply rather than risk having a shortage,” said Tiu Laurel.
Tiu Laurel noted that increased rice imports for the year will also serve as a supply cushion for the first quarter of next year in order to get ahead of a potentially weaker harvest season.
Considering this, the import volume for 2027 may go down to the normal range of between 3.8 million MT and four million MT.
While the country relies on foreign supplies to meet domestic demand, Tiu Laurel said the main objective of the government continues to be increasing local output.
He told lawmakers that the DA is focused on rolling out mechanization measures, expanding irrigation, and developing new rice seeds to further boost productivity.
The agency is also preparing to implement a program requiring traders to first invest in rice mills and processing facilities before they allowed to purchase rice from abroad.
It is estimated that around 80 percent of rice importers in the country are engaged solely in importing and have yet to commit investments in the local rice sector.
“That is one of the plans to make the industry self-sustaining and competitive in the international market,” said Tiu Laurel.
Based on BPI data, Vietnam has maintained its position as the country’s top rice supplier with imports reaching 2.56 million MT, or 74 percent of the total volume, as of Aug. 13.
Other top sources of rice include Thailand with 378,404 MT, Myanmar with 286,052 MT, Pakistan with 107,485 MT, and Cambodia with 87,802 MT.
The DA’s proposed budget for next year is ₱198.45 billion, down eight percent from the allocation of ₱215.69 billion for this year.

Under this budget, the agency wants to prioritize programs that raise farm and fishery productivity, improve infrastructure, reduce post-harvest losses, strengthen logistics and market access, and expand the use of technology.

articles.title: Creamline stays unscathed; EST Cola sweeps Farm Fresh
articles.summary: Creamline routed Ho Chih Minh City, 25-18, 25-16, 25-6, to remain unscathed, while EST Cola swept Farm Fresh, 25-21, 25-16, 25-22, to barge into the win column in the PVL Invitational at the Smart…

blocks.text: Creamline routed Ho Chih Minh City, 25-18, 25-16, 25-6, to remain unscathed, while EST Cola swept Farm Fresh, 25-21, 25-16, 25-22, to barge into the win column in the PVL Invitational at the Smart Araneta Coliseumon Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The Cool Smashers exposed the Vietnamese’s lethargic plays, needing 61 minutes to dominate the guest team for their second straight win in as many outings.
Tots Carlos, Jema Galanza and Jaja Santiago-Minowa paced Creamline with 12 points apiece, including combined 21 kills from Carlos and Galanza, and three blocks from Santiago-Minowa.
So dominant were the Cool Smashers that they overpowered the Vietnamese spikers on attacks, 49-19; blocks, 11-4; and aces, 5-3.
None from Ho Chi Minh City scored in twin figures with skipper Dang Thi Kim Thanh and Le Thi My Xuyen pacing only eight and six points, respectively, as they absorbed their second straight loss.
Earlier, EST Cola made its title bid to improve its record to 1-1 behind the efforts of Papatchaya Phontham.
Phontham blasted 17 points built on 13 kills, three aces and one block to shackle Farm Fresh, which struggled despite the 15-point effort of Trisha Tubu.

articles.title: Yamsuan bent on helping CHEd once travel tax windfall stops
articles.summary: A solon who holds a key position in the House 2027 national budget process has vowed to help find alternative funding for the Commission on Higher Education (CHEd) should the measure abolishing the…

blocks.text: A solon who holds a key position in the House 2027 national budget process has vowed to help find alternative funding for the Commission on Higher Education (CHEd) should the measure abolishing the travel tax becomes a law this year.

Parañaque City 2nd district Rep. Brian Raymund Yamsuan has noted that CHEd, which regulates higher education and administers the government’s financial aid programs for tertiary-level students, gets part of its funding from 40 percent of the total gross collections from the travel tax.

Yamsuan, a member of the House Budget Amendments and Review Subcommittee (BARSc) pointed out that under Malacañang’s National Expenditure Program for Fiscal Year 2027, a portion of the allocation for the CHEd’s Higher Education Development Fund (HEDF) would still be sourced from the travel tax collections of the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA).

“Kami po ay magtatrabaho sa Kongreso para hanapan kayo ng alternative sources of funding once mangyari po ang pagsasabatas ng abolition ng travel tax,” Yamsuan told CHEd Chairperson Shirley Agrupis during the House Committee on Appropriations’ recent budget deliberations on the agency’s proposed 2027 budget.
(We will work in Congress to look for alternative sources of funding once the travel tax measure is enacted into law.)

Formed during last year's budget cycle as a pro-transparency measure, the BARSc effectively replaced the so-called "small committee", which incorporates individual ammendments to the General Appropriations Bill (GAB) or proposed national budget.

If the bill abolishing the travel tax is passed into law, Agrupis told the House Committee on Tourism last March that without a substitute funding source, the CHEd would lose 85.6 percent of the funding for the HEDF.
She calls this prospect “a structural loss that directly affects scholarships, research and institutional upgrading, and tourism education programs".

The House of Representatives approved on March 16 the measure seeking to abolish the travel tax. Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian earlier said the Senate version of the measure is included in the chamber’s priority list of bills and will be passed this year.

“Kami bilang member ng BARSc, sisiguraduhin ko po na sa susunod na pagpupulong with (Committee on Appropriations) Chair Mika (Suansing) ay gagawa po kami ng paraan upang maibalik ang pondo para hindi maantala ang magagandang programa ng CHEd,” Yamsuan added.

(As member of the BARSc, I would make sure that in the next meeting with Committee on Appropriations Chairperson Mikaela Angela Suansing, we would find ways to restore CHEd’s funding so as not to delay the implementation of CHEd’s good programs)

During the hearing, the Parañaque solon also thanked the CHEd for its efficient implementation of the government’s higher education initiatives and financial assistance to tertiary-level students, particularly the Tulong Dunong Program (TDP).
The TDP provides a financial grant of up to P7,500 per semester or a total of P15,000 per school year to help cover the tuition and other daily expenses of qualified college students.
Yamsuan urged the CHEd to conduct more consultations with Local Universities and Colleges (LUC) to help them institute reforms that would allow them to take part in the TDP.
Out of 170 LUCs, only 116 are CHEd-recognized institutions qualified to accept TDP grants from its enrollees.

articles.title: On the borderline
articles.summary: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean. "Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim Think of…

blocks.text: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean.
"Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim

Think of the immigrant experience, but now seen through a SciFi lens, and you have an idea of what this novel bravely explores. Kim has written short stories that have won Nebula, Locus, and Shirley Jackson Awards, and this is her debut novel. Soyoung Rose Kang is the protagonist here, and at the age of 10, she left Korea with her mother to emigrate to the USA. She left an ‘instance’ in Korea, who would continue to interact with her family and grandfather. And now, with the death of the grandfather, Soyoung (the instance in Korea) gets in touch with Rose (the instance in the USA), to let her know it was their grandfather’s wish that she come to Seoul for the funeral. What Rose isn’t aware of is that Soyoung harbors the desire to reintegrate. This gets complicated by the fact that the grandfather has left his house to Rose - who never tried to establish a relationship with Soyoung, or her ‘lolo’.

Structured initially so that the chapters alternate between Soyoung and Rose’s POVs, Kim pulls off this delicate balancing act with a lot of skill and charm. She endeavors to make both Soyoung and Rose distinct, while also having such similarities so we appreciate how they are, in fact, two versions of the same person. They’re not twins or doppelgangers, but two ‘instances’-and before the grandfather’s death and meeting in Seoul, have not really been in contact with each other. To make our reading more intense, there’s a Yujin in Korea, and his instance, YJ, in New York. Childhood friend of Soyoung, the Yujin pair have their own set of issues, but have been friends since the moment of ‘instance’, communicating regularly. Their story and how it intersects with that of Soyoung Rose take up the last half of this novel, which takes us to some hard decision-making and the facing of consequences. Bold, imaginative writing that speaks of borders and identity.
"The Pinnacle" by Abir Mukhergee

Set in the penthouse of a luxury condominium called The Pinnacle in Mumbai, this new novel from the author of Hunted, which was named 2025 Thriller of the Year, is both a locked-room mystery thriller and a penetrating study of class dynamics in India today. George Abercrombie is an over-the-hill Hollywood actor who’s married to Sweety Sahota, the current queen of Bollywood. Gemma is Sweety’s PA who joined them in India all the way from the US. The premise has to do with George waking up after a quarrel with Sweety and a drinking binge, and finding her murdered on their king-size bed. With no recollection of what he did the night before, one narrative strand has to do with George having to prove he’s innocent. Then there’s Gemma, who’s receiving cryptic text messages. And finally, there’s Amit, George’s shadow and PA, who seems to know too much and goes on the run.

The seedy underbelly of luxury living is exposed in this gripping adventure. We may be on the 68th floor of an upscale skyscraper, but the hypocrisy, filth, and societal evil still reach these heights. The novel revolves around three plots, and the borders of society and social standing are constantly placed as reminders of what our protagonists have to face on a Daily basis. As in Hunted, Mukhergee is excellent at piling on the action and turning the screws tighter as the novel enters the home stretch. If you’re the type who reads late at night before getting a good night’s sleep, be forewarned that this is a biting thriller, and you’ll be reluctant to put it down, as you’ll be wanting to know what happens next. It’s that well-paced. I would not be surprised if both Hollywood and Bollywood will go bidding for the movie rights to this book; and I know I’ll be looking forward to its film adaptation, and the casting.
"The Lighthouse At the End of the World" by Philip A. Suggars

Think Oliver Twist, but updated for today’s London; then add a spice of portal-esque fantasy - and you’ll have an idea of just how original an adventure this debut novel of Suggars is. It's Charles Dickens meets SciFi, and Oyster McCellan is our scrappy 15-year-old guide to this nifty piece of world-building - two distinct worlds, to be exact. First time we meet Oyster, he’s a member of the Urbans, a small-time gang of grifters who operate around Westminster, hoping to fleece unsuspecting tourists. His father, Lucas, was formerly the head of the gang, but he disappeared without any explanation. So now Oyster has to earn a keep, to help his sister Cecile continue her studies, and their mother Paris, who is still in something of a daze. It’s when a money drop goes terribly wrong that Oyster finds himself in an alternate Greater London.

The novel is familial trauma mixed with immersive world-building. Greater London is a version where leviathans roam the seas, and strangely sympathetic and communicating ink beetles nestle beneath the skin of Oyster’s armpit. Plus there looms the nagging question of whether his father Lucas escaped here, and what his role is in the scheme of things. Meanwhile, as we join Oyster, our tourist guide to Greater London, we encounter the enigma Nonesuch, a female practitioner of rappelling and scavenging skills, the escapist Marya Petrovna who seems to take Oyster under her protective wing but for what deeper purpose, and the terrifying Mr. Primrose, who seems to have his finger on all of Oyster’s movements between worlds, and seems to have confederates from within Oyster’s own gang of Urbans. There’s so much to relish and enjoy as we suspend disbelief and surrender to Suggars' vision and world-building.

articles.title: Philippines, Nigeria can develop, explore many opportunities — Marcos
articles.summary: The Philippines and Nigeria can explore and develop many opportunities, President Marcos said as he welcomed Nigeria’s new ambassador to the country. Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of…

blocks.text: The Philippines and Nigeria can explore and develop many opportunities, President Marcos said as he welcomed Nigeria’s new ambassador to the country.

Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Federal Republic of Nigeria to the Republic of the Philippines Ibok-Ete Ekwe Ibas presented his Letter of Credence to Marcos at Malacañan Palace on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
During the presentation of credentials, Marcos told the Nigerian envoy that their countries can potentially expand their partnership in energy security, trade, and investment.

"The Philippines and Nigeria have significant potential to expand cooperation especially in energy security, trade and investment, and pursue initiatives that would mutually benefit our peoples and our countries," Marcos said.
"There are many things that, in my view, we can explore and develop. There are so many opportunities that will be of mutual benefit to both our countries," the President added.
"During your tenure as Ambassador, I look forward to further strengthening bilateral relations between our two countries," Marcos also said.
Marcos further said he looks forward to working with the Nigerian ambassador to promote and deepen the Philippines' and Nigeria's collaboration and cooperation, which has spanned 64 years.
Ambassador Ibas, for his part, assured the President that he would work hard to strengthen the friendly, strong bilateral relations between the two countries.
Ibas was joined by his wife and other Embassy officials during the ceremony.
Also present during the event were Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, DFA Assistant Secretary Germinia Aguilar-Usudan, and Deputy Chief of Presidential Protocol Dennis Briones.
The Philippines and Nigeria established diplomatic relations on August 1, 1962, and will mark 65 years of diplomatic relations in 2027.

articles.title: Severe offenders face exclusion: DepEd tightens penalties for bullying, violence, threats in schools
articles.summary: Learners who commit severe acts of bullying, physical assault, or threats may face immediate exclusion, non-readmission, and mandatory referral to law enforcement or social welfare authorities under…

blocks.text: (PHOTO: PIXABAY)

Learners who commit severe acts of bullying, physical assault, or threats may face immediate exclusion, non-readmission, and mandatory referral to law enforcement or social welfare authorities under stricter Department of Education (DepEd) rules.

This was the agency’s warning as it formalized consolidated learner protection protocols under DepEd Order No. 006, s. 2026, or the Guidelines on Ensuring a Safe and Motivating Learning Environment (ESMLE).

According to DepEd, its campaign against violence and classroom disruptions is being implemented in coordination with partner agencies, local government units (LGUs), law enforcement authorities, and local communities.
While learners deserve an opportunity to change, Angara said DepEd would never put the safety of the majority at risk.
“Ang paaralan ay dapat maging ligtas at tahimik na lugar para sa lahat (Schools should be safe and peaceful places for everyone),” he said in a statement.
The education department said severe offenses will prompt immediate inter-agency action under the policy.
